## A 1U rectifier board is a thermal part with a circuit attached

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/1u-rectifier-thermal-joint.html
Published: 2026-11-19
Summary: A rack rectifier is a PFC stage and a DC-DC stage on one heatsink, and the failure that matters is invisible from above. Where the build risk sits on a 1U power board.

A 1U rectifier module is usually described by its output — 3 kW, 48 V, 97 % efficient. Almost none of that is decided on the assembly floor. What is decided on the assembly floor is whether the joint under the switching devices and the thermal pad between the board and the heatsink is continuous, because that joint is what the efficiency figure quietly depends on.

This is the one board family where the inspection step, not the placement step, is the interesting part of the quotation.

### What is on the board

Two power stages and a control section, usually on one board:

- PFC front end. Boost stage, bridge or bridgeless, with the inductor and the current sense. This is the part that decides input current shape and therefore whether the unit passes harmonic limits.
- DC-DC stage. Isolated converter producing the 48 V or 12 V bus, with synchronous rectification on the secondary.
- Auxiliary supply. The small converter that keeps the control alive when the main stage is off. Cheap, hot, and the usual cause of a unit that will not start.
- Control and telemetry. The MCU, the PMBus or CAN interface, and the fan and hot-swap logic that makes a shelf of these behave.

Dense, double-sided, heavy copper on the power side, and fine-pitch on the control side. Both extremes on one panel is what makes the stencil and the reflow profile a compromise rather than an optimisation.

### The void you cannot see

Under a power MOSFET or a rectifier in a QFN or LFPAK, the thermal pad is the only path to the copper. If the paste coverage under that pad is 60 % instead of 90 %, the board passes every electrical test at room temperature and runs twenty degrees hotter in a shelf. Nothing on the top side shows it. AOI sees the fillet, not the void.

X-ray is how that joint is judged, and on this product it is read by an operator against a limit rather than accepted on a green light. That is the one inspection step on this family that a buyer should ask about by name, because a line that has X-ray and a line that reads X-ray are not the same supplier.

The same reasoning applies to the interface between the board and the heatsink: the pad or the paste, the flatness of the board, and the torque on the mounting screws. A warped board with a good pad still leaves an air gap in the middle.

### Thick copper changes the reflow profile, not the placement

Power boards carry 2 to 4 oz copper on the power side and 1 oz on the control side. The thermal mass difference across one panel means the profile has to be developed for that board, not reused from the previous job. That is one honest reason a first run is more expensive than the second: the profile work happens once, and it happens properly or it happens again.

On this floor the profile is developed per board and the first article is X-rayed and photographed before the lot proceeds.

### Where the high-current path lands

The 48 V output leaves the board through busbar tabs, press-fit pins, or screw terminals. All three are mechanical joints with an electrical job:

- Press-fit needs the right hole tolerance and the right insertion tool; a reamed hole gives you a joint that passes and later opens.
- Screw terminals need a specified torque and a washer that does not cold-flow.
- Solder tabs on thick copper need enough heat and enough time, and both are limited by what the parts nearby will survive.

These are specified on your drawing and executed here. If the drawing does not specify the torque or the press-fit force, the build will use a house default, and a house default is not a design decision.

### Coating on a rack power board

Most 1U rectifiers are not coated. The airflow through the shelf is the environmental control, and coating the power side adds thermal resistance exactly where the design cannot afford it. Where coating does appear is on the control and telemetry side, or on units sold into humid or coastal sites.

That is a callout to make deliberately: what is coated, what is masked, and why the power side is excluded. A blanket "conformal coat, whole board" on a 3 kW module is a thermal decision made by accident.

Potting is not done here, and on this family that is rarely a loss — the enclosure and the airflow are doing the work.

### What an assembler cannot measure for you

The number on the datasheet is efficiency at a defined load, and it is measured on a load bank with power analysers, at temperature, over time. That measurement happens at the module designer, not here.

So the honest scope line on a rectifier enquiry is: placed, reflowed, X-rayed on the thermal joints, inspected, recorded. Not characterised. If your qualification plan needs the efficiency curve from the build lot rather than the design, that is a test house or your own bench, and it is worth saying so before the order rather than after.

The same applies to hold-up time, inrush, conducted emissions and transient response. All of them are properties of the design, exercised on equipment this floor does not have.

### What records matter here

- X-ray images of the thermal-pad joints, per device type, filed against the lot
- The reflow profile used, with the board revision it was developed for
- First-article photographs of the busbar or press-fit joints before and after insertion
- SPI results on the fine-pitch side, since a thin print there is a separate failure from a void

### What to send for a quote

The BOM with the power devices named by package and not just by part number, the copper weights per layer, the stack-up, the drawing showing the thermal interface and the mounting torque, the connector and busbar list, and the quantity per variant.

The family page for this product is AI and data centre power boards (/applications/ai-power.html). For the inspection question in general, what AOI and X-ray still cannot catch (/insights/what-aoi-xray-cannot-catch.html) is the companion note, and what a PCBA quote should contain (/insights/pcba-quote-what-it-should-contain.html) covers the scope lines that keep this kind of order honest.

## On an AMR the connector fails before the solder joint does

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/amr-connector-is-the-failure-point.html
Published: 2026-11-19
Summary: Drive, battery and sensor boards in a vehicle that gets serviced. The failure that matters is mechanical, and it is decided by connector choice and coating, not by placement.

An AMR or AGV carries two to four boards: a drive board per wheel pair or per motor, a battery interface board, and something that talks to the sensors. A fleet is a hundred robots; a hundred robots is four hundred boards, then another four hundred when the fleet doubles.

The boards are not the hard part. The hard part is that every one of them is inside a vehicle that gets opened, serviced, unplugged and pushed by a technician in a warehouse at eleven at night. The joint that fails in that story is almost never a solder joint.

### Two or four drives, one battery interface

The drive boards are power boards with isolation between the control side and the motor side, current sense and a brake or enable path. The battery board is the interesting one: 48 V nominal, contactor or MOSFET disconnect, pre-charge if the design has it, and a sense chain that has to be accurate at both ends of the state of charge.

That mix means one build carries three different risks at once:

Board: Dominant risk · Where it is decided
Drive: Thermal path under the bridge, isolation spacing · Stack-up, paste volume, reflow profile
Battery interface: Creepage at 48–58 V, contactor joint quality · Drawing, through-hole fill, torque spec
Sensor / comms: Connector integrity, EMI · Connector choice, shielding, coating

A quote that prices all three as "boards" without separating them hides exactly the part you need to manage.

### The connector is the failure point, not the placement

A robot board gets unplugged far more often than a consumer board. Three consequences, all decided before the order:

- Latched, keyed, and rated for cycles. A connector that is not rated for the number of mating cycles the service procedure implies is a warranty cost with a part number.
- Strain relief at the board edge. A harness in a robot hangs and moves. A connector held only by its solder joints is a cold joint waiting for its third service visit.
- Field-replaceable without a soldering iron. If a technician has to rework the board in the field, the design has already lost.

Coating enters the same argument: it buys tolerance to dust and condensation, and it does nothing for a housing that takes water. On a warehouse floor with a wash-down next door, that distinction is the whole reliability question.

### Prototype to fleet: what changes with volume

At 100 to 1,000 sets, small-volume habits carry a programme a long way. What changes as the fleet grows is not the placement difficulty but the amount of information you need per unit — and that is where an assembler without in-circuit test becomes a problem you have to plan around rather than discover.

There is no in-circuit test and no functional test on this floor. If the fleet needs per-serial electrical proof, the fixture and the programme are yours to specify, and the arrangement has to be in writing before the first build. That is a workable arrangement; an unstated one is not.

### Where this floor stops

- Vehicle-level safety certification and the standards file. That sits with the robot builder and a test house.
- Motor-load test on a running chassis, and any in-house in-circuit or functional test.
- Potting, encapsulation, or bonding the board to a thermal chassis.
- Underfill or staking as a standard step. It is agreed per design at DFM, never assumed.

### What to send for a quote

Gerber with the stack-up and the isolation drawing, the BOM, the centroid, the connector list with mating halves and cycle ratings, the through-hole joint callouts with torque where relevant, the coating and mask list, and the quantity per board type. At 100 to 1,000 sets the build is three working days from kitted parts.

The family page is AMR and AGV drive and battery boards (/applications/amr-agv.html). If per-serial electrical proof matters to your fleet, what to do when your assembler has no in-circuit test (/insights/in-circuit-test-outsourcing.html) is the note to read before the order, and what a PCBA quote should contain (/insights/pcba-quote-what-it-should-contain.html) covers the scope lines.

## A car amplifier is a power supply with an audio problem, and the yield number is voiding

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/car-amplifier-voids-not-watts.html
Published: 2026-11-19
Summary: A Class-D amplifier board is judged on heat before it is judged on sound. Where the build risk sits, why variants are the trap, and what the bench here cannot tell you.

An aftermarket car amplifier is a switching power supply feeding a Class-D output stage, in a box that lives in a boot, under a parcel shelf, in a car that gets to 60 °C in summer. The board is heavy copper, snap-in electrolytics, clamped power devices and a thermal path into a finned aluminium case.

Buyers describe it in watts and distortion. The board does not know about either. What it knows about is heat, and the part of the heat path that assembly controls is the part nobody can inspect afterwards.

### Voiding under the power devices is the whole yield number

A Class-D output stage and the supply's switching devices are packaged to conduct their heat into the board, and then into the case. If the thermal pad under a device has 60 % coverage instead of 90 %, three things follow, in this order:

- The device runs hotter than designed, in a box that is already hot.
- It derates, or the protection trips earlier than the specification says.
- In the worst case it fails, and the failure is attributed to the design rather than to a joint.

None of that is visible. AOI sees the fillet, not the void. X-ray sees the void, which is why X-ray on the power joints is the inspection that decides shipment on this family — and why "we have X-ray" and "we read X-ray against a limit" are different claims.

### The thermal path is half mechanical, and half of it is not measured here

The board-to-case interface is a pad or a paste, a flatness requirement, and a torque specification on the mounting screws. All three are drawing items that get executed here. None of them can be verified here, because verification is a temperature measurement under load, and there is no chamber, no thermocouple instrumentation and no load measurement on this floor.

That leaves the buyer with a practical choice: either the thermal design has margin that does not depend on measuring every unit, or the measurement happens at your end-of-line. Assuming the assembler measured it is the one option that does not exist.

### What is not measured: watts, distortion, noise, efficiency

The whole audio and power claim is outside this building:

- Audio measurement of any kind — output power, distortion, noise, efficiency, DSP tuning, acoustic verification.
- Thermal verification of the assembled amplifier.
- EMC pre-compliance or compliance testing for a switching amplifier, and any certified report.
- Potting or encapsulation, and ingress testing of the finished chassis.

For a brand whose selling point is a number on a box, that means the acceptance plan is yours, and it is worth being explicit about which units get measured and what happens to the ones that are not.

### Five hundred to five thousand pieces, and the variants are the trap

At 500 to 5,000 pcs this family is comfortable for a high-mix floor. The trap is not volume, it is variety: one platform shipping as four power levels, two channel counts and three cosmetic variants, each with a different BOM and sometimes a different board.

Two habits keep that manageable:

- Keep the board revision count low and push variants into the BOM where the design allows it. Every board revision re-opens stencil, profile and first article.
- Batch the variants rather than interleaving them. Changeover is the cost that gets hidden in a blended unit price and then discovered when the schedule compresses.

### Where this floor stops

- Any audio or thermal measurement.
- EMC testing and certification.
- Potting, encapsulation and chassis assembly.
- Volumes far above five thousand a month, where a dedicated line wins on unit price.

### What to send for a quote

Gerber with copper weights and the stack-up, the BOM with the power devices named by package, the centroid, the thermal interface and mounting torque callout, the terminal and connector list, the coating callout if used, and the quantity per variant with the variant matrix. At 500 to 5,000 pcs a build is three working days from kitted parts.

The family page is car audio, DSP and Class-D amplifier boards (/applications/car-audio.html). The same voiding argument on a denser power board is in the 1U rectifier thermal joint (/insights/1u-rectifier-thermal-joint.html), and the inspection limits are in what AOI and X-ray can and cannot catch (/insights/what-aoi-xray-cannot-catch.html).

## On a DC fast charger the power modules are bought — the control board is what you are specifying

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/dc-charger-built-vs-bought.html
Published: 2026-11-19
Summary: The conversion stage arrives as a module with somebody else's name on it. What a contract assembler actually contributes to a DC charger, and the three places the build can still go wrong.

A DC fast charger is often described as if it were one product built in one place. It is not. The conversion stage — the AC-to-DC power modules that make the cabinet a charger — arrives as a sealed module with a datasheet, a manufacturer and its own certification. What is left, and what a contract assembler actually builds, is the control board, the metering board and the interface board, plus the harness and the high-current path that join them.

Understanding that split is the difference between specifying a buildable order and discovering at type test that nobody owned the interface.

### What the cabinet is made of

Four groups of parts, four different owners:

Part: Who supplies it · What that means for your order
Power modules: A module vendor, certified as a unit · Not assembled here; their efficiency and safety claims are theirs
Control board: Assembled here to your design · Runs the state machine, the insulation monitoring inputs, the lock and the session
Metering board: Assembled here, calibrated and certified elsewhere · Accuracy is a certification question, not an assembly one
Interface and HMI: Assembled here, or bought as a module · Often the cheapest thing to buy whole and the easiest to build badly

If your supplier quotes you "a charger", ask which of those four lines they are actually performing.

### The control board is where the integration risk lands

The control board is the one part of the cabinet that has to talk to everything the buyer did not design: the module vendor's CAN protocol, the vehicle over the charging standard, the site over the network, and the safety chain over discrete inputs.

That is a firmware integration job with an assembly job underneath it. What arrives at an assembler is the finished design; what leaves is a board that has been placed, reflowed, coated, inspected and recorded. The protocol conformance is a test the charger builder runs, and no assembler can substitute for it.

Where the assembly does affect the outcome is signal integrity on the isolated interfaces, connector quality on the harness side, and whether the coating callout survives an outdoor cabinet. Those are the three we can speak to.

### The high-current path is a mechanical problem wearing an electrical costume

The DC output path — busbars, terminal blocks, contactor lugs — is through-hole and heavy copper. On this floor that is selective or hand solder with the thermal mass managed per joint, and the first article is inspected by cross-section and pull rather than by a green light on an AOI screen.

Three things go wrong here repeatedly:

- Insufficient fill on a lug. Looks soldered, measures cold, heats under load.
- Torque applied to a joint instead of a stud. The joint survives the build and fails in service.
- Plating and paste mismatch on a thick terminal. No amount of reflow tuning fixes a surface that will not wet.

None of these is caught by AOI. They are caught by specifying the joint, then inspecting it the way the specification says.

### Metering is a certificate, not a calibration step

A charger that bills for energy carries a meter that has to be accurate to a defined class, and that accuracy is certified by a body against a standard. Assembling the metering board is not the same as certifying the meter, and no contract assembler should let a buyer believe otherwise.

The practical consequence: the metering board is usually bought as a certified sub-assembly, or assembled and then sent for certification by the charger builder. If a quotation offers you "metering included" without naming who issues the certificate, that is the question to ask.

### Coating on an outdoor cabinet

Chargers live outdoors, often at the coast, and conformal coating is standard on the control and interface boards. It is done here with the connectors and the test points masked by hand.

What coating buys is tolerance to condensation and pollution on a board inside an enclosure that breathes. What it does not buy is an enclosure rating. A cabinet that takes water at the door gasket will take it regardless of what is on the board, and the coating callout should be written for the environment the board sees, not as a substitute for sealing the box.

Potting is the other option and it is not done here. A control board potted into an enclosure is a different process with a different repair story, and it belongs with whoever owns the enclosure.

### What records matter on this product

Because the failure modes are thermal and mechanical rather than electronic, the records that matter are the ones that show a joint was made properly:

- First-article cross-section on the DC output lugs and the contactor joints
- The selective-solder program revision and the nozzle set used
- Coating record with the mask list, and where the mask was verified
- SPI and AOI results per lot, filed rather than summarised

On a charger these are worth more than a functional pass count, because the board can pass at room temperature and fail at the output current it was designed for.

### Where this floor stops

- No type test, no EMC test, no safety certification. Those run at an accredited laboratory against the charging standard the market requires, on the finished cabinet.
- No efficiency or thermal measurement of the conversion stage. The modules are the vendor's; the load bank that would measure them is not here.
- No metering certification. See above.
- No enclosure assembly or sealing. We build and coat boards and see them into the box; the box is the charger builder's.

### What to send for a quote

Board drawings with the current-carrying joints called out, the stack-up, the connector and terminal list with the mating half named, the coating callout and mask list, and the quantity per variant. If the metering board is supplied by you as a certified assembly, say so and we will quote it as a handled item rather than a build.

The AC side of the same story is in the EVSE audit record set (/insights/evse-audit-record-set.html), and the family pages are DC charger boards (/applications/dc-charger.html) and AC wallbox boards (/applications/evse.html). For why a first run costs more than the second, see why the second run costs less (/insights/why-the-second-run-costs-less.html).

## A flight controller is one IMU away from being scrap, and nobody here can tell you which one

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/flight-controller-imu-calibration-boundary.html
Published: 2026-11-19
Summary: The flight controller is a small board whose hardest requirement is a sensor alignment done somewhere else. What to specify here, and what belongs to the aircraft maker.

A drone programme usually arrives as three boards: a flight controller, an ESC or ESC-per-arm, and something for the payload. None of them is hard to place. What makes the flight controller different from every other fine-pitch board on this site is that its most important property — where the inertial sensor actually sits and which way it points — is fixed by a calibration step that happens in the airframe, long after the board was inspected and packed.

That has a consequence buyers should hear before the order rather than after: this floor can build a board that calibrates cleanly, and cannot tell you whether it did.

### What a flight controller is, physically

A small board, usually four to six layers, with a fine-pitch IMU at the centre, a barometer, a magnetometer if the design carries one, and a connector set that has to survive being plugged and unplugged by somebody with cold hands in a field.

Three things on it decide whether the build is repeatable:

- The IMU's placement relative to the board datum. Not the absolute position — the consistency of it, board to board, so that the airframe calibration offsets stay in a narrow window.
- Strain around the IMU. A board that flexes under a mounting screw transmits that flex into the sensor. Where the mounting holes sit relative to the part is a layout decision; how much paste and how much reflow stress land on the part is an assembly one.
- The connector and pad finish. A USB or SWD connector that lifts a pad on the third reflash is a bricked board, and it happens after your test, not during it.

### The ESC board is the opposite problem in the same airframe

The ESC is heavy copper, big FETs, high current, and thermal management into an arm that is often carbon fibre with poor conductivity in the direction you need. It is a power board with a narrow margin in a very small volume.

Board: What decides it · What assembly controls · What it cannot
Flight controller: Sensor placement and firmware · Paste volume, reflow profile, strain around the IMU, connector integrity · Calibration, sensor fusion, flight behaviour
ESC: Thermal path and current density · Voiding under the FETs, heavy-copper joint quality, coating if specified · Thrust, timing, motor compatibility
Payload: Interface and power budget · The same as any mixed-signal board · Whatever the payload does

The two boards fail for reasons that never overlap, which is why a single "drone PCBA" quote that does not separate them is a quote you cannot audit.

### What inspection proves here, and what it does not

SPI before reflow, AOI after, X-ray on the IMU and the ESC power joints, and first-article photographs. That set proves the board was assembled to the drawing and that the joints under the parts you cannot see are formed.

It does not prove the IMU is straight in the way that matters. Tilt of a fraction of a degree is invisible to X-ray and readable only by the airframe calibration routine. If your yield model assumes the board is "good" because it passed inspection, the model is missing the step that actually decides it.

This is also why a returned-board argument is worth settling in writing: if a drone flies badly, the board, the calibration and the airframe are three suspects, and only one of them was ever in this building.

### Where this floor stops

- Inertial calibration, sensor-fusion tuning and flight test. These belong to the aircraft maker, who owns the fixture and the firmware.
- Radio, EMC, and any airworthiness or spectrum approval for the finished aircraft.
- AS9100 process control, NADCAP special processes, ITAR-registered and export-controlled programme handling. None of these are held here, and a defence or restricted programme should not start with this floor.
- Potting or encapsulation of a board. Coating is what happens here.

### What to send for a quote

Gerber with the stack-up, the BOM with the IMU and any alternate named exactly, the centroid, the connector list with the mating half, the coating callout if the ESC is coated, and the quantity split across the two or three boards. At 100 to 1,000 sets the build is three working days from kitted parts, so the clock that actually matters is component lead time, not the line.

The family page is UAV and flight controller boards (/applications/uav.html). For what inspection genuinely covers, see what AOI and X-ray can and cannot catch (/insights/what-aoi-xray-cannot-catch.html); for the lead-time argument, the four clocks inside a PCBA lead time (/insights/four-clocks-in-a-pcba-lead-time.html).

## On a GNSS board the RF section is a keep-out, and assembly is what quietly breaks it

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/gnss-rf-section-keep-out.html
Published: 2026-11-19
Summary: Fifty to five hundred boards a year, an RF front end nobody here can measure, and a coating decision that can detune it. Where the build risk actually sits.

A GNSS receiver or telemetry board has an RF front end, a baseband or module, and an interface section, often with a shield can over the front end and a coax pigtail to the antenna connector on the enclosure. Volume is fifty to five hundred a year. The boards are not hard to place.

What makes this family worth its own note is that the things assembly can do to an RF front end are invisible to every test on this floor, and that the buyer usually learns about them from a position accuracy complaint rather than from incoming inspection.

### The RF section is a keep-out, not a component list

Three areas need to be treated as protected rather than merely populated:

- Under and around the shield can. Ground pads have to be fully formed before the can goes on; a void there is an RF ground that is not a ground. That is an X-ray check, done before the can is fitted, not after.
- The antenna feed and matching network. Solder mask, coating and flux residue around the feed change impedance. The mask drawing should say what stays bare, and the process should respect it.
- The keep-out around the antenna itself. Any metal added near the radiating element — a stray solder ball, a shield fence in the wrong place — detunes it, and the tuning was done by somebody else, at design time.

The general rule for this family: everything near the RF section is either specified or it is a variable.

### Coax pigtails, connectors and heat

A board with a coax pigtail has a joint that is both electrical and mechanical, and it usually takes a small amount of heat in a small area:

- Connector-to-board joints need the right amount of solder and the right amount of heat. Too little is intermittent; too much damages the dielectric inside the connector, which shows up as loss rather than as an open.
- The pigtail is a handle. Whoever assembles the unit will lift the board by it at least once. Strain relief is a drawing item.
- Sealing at the enclosure. The connector bulkhead seal belongs to the enclosure, not to the board, and the two need to be designed together.

### What is not measured, and what that costs the buyer

Nothing on this floor measures the RF chain. Specifically:

- No RF alignment, antenna characterisation, or position accuracy and time-to-first-fix measurement.
- No EMC pre-compliance, no environmental qualification such as MIL-STD-810 or IP ratings, and no certified test report.
- No ITAR-registered handling, classified work, or cryptography approval / Type-1 requirements.
- No functional test of any kind, including a simple "does it acquire satellites" check.

For a buyer, the practical consequence is that the acceptance plan has to run somewhere else. Fifty boards a year is an awkward volume for a test house, which is exactly why the fixture question is worth settling at the quotation stage rather than after the first batch — the same economics that make a small-run fixture a fixed cost.

### Fifty to five hundred a year, and that is the point

This band is not a stepping stone for most GNSS programmes; it is the steady state, because the products are specialised instruments with long lives and few variants. The right supplier is one set up for a reorder that looks exactly like the previous one, with the records to prove it.

At that cadence, the most valuable thing an assembler provides is continuity: the same stencil, the same profile, the same coating mask set, documented, so board nineteen matches board one.

### Where this floor stops

- RF characterisation in all its forms — alignment, antenna, accuracy, TTFF.
- EMC, environmental and certified testing.
- ITAR, classified and export-controlled programme handling.
- Volumes above a few thousand a year where the assembler is expected to run functional test.

### What to send for a quote

Gerber with the stack-up and the RF region marked, the BOM with the front end and module named, the centroid, the can and ground-pad drawing, the coax pigtail and connector list, the coating and mask drawing with the keep-out areas explicit, and the quantity. At 50 to 500 sets a build is three working days from kitted parts.

The family page is GNSS, telemetry and ground station boards (/applications/gnss.html). For the shield-can rework path in a rugged device, where the coating is the product (/insights/rugged-radio-coating-is-the-product.html); for the inspection order of operations, what AOI and X-ray can and cannot catch (/insights/what-aoi-xray-cannot-catch.html).

## The number a home battery is judged on is measured in microamps, and there is no microamp bench here

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/home-battery-microamp-standby.html
Published: 2026-11-19
Summary: A home stack is judged on the days it does nothing. Where the assembly affects standby current, and which parts of the approval file never touch this building.

A residential battery spends most of its life doing nothing. It charges in the morning, discharges in the evening, and then sits — for eighteen hours a day, for a decade — drawing a standby current that decides how much of the installed capacity the owner actually gets to use. Buyers argue about that number in datasheets and reviews. It is measured in microamps, and there is no microamp bench in this building.

That is worth saying at the top, because the rest of the page is about the parts of a home stack that assembly genuinely decides.

### Four boards, and only one is a power board

A hybrid home system is typically a module BMU, an inverter control board, a stack master and a communication board.

- The module BMU measures cell voltages and pack temperature and balances. It is repeated per module, so a defect is multiplied.
- The inverter control board is the one that looks like a power board: gate drive, current sense, the isolated sensing chain that has to stay honest across a decade.
- The stack master coordinates modules and enforces the disconnect logic. It is the board that has to be right when something else is wrong.
- The communication board is the cheapest and the one most likely to be replaced mid-life, which is an argument for connectors that survive being unplugged ten times.

### Sensing that has to stay honest for years

The voltage and current sense chain is a low-drift analogue problem, and the assembly contribution is not glamorous:

- Cleanliness. Leakage across residue shows up as drift, not as a dead board.
- Thermal symmetry. Two sense paths in different thermal environments read differently, and the layout decides that.
- Coating, with the sense area treated deliberately. Coating protects; coating over a humidity-sensitive divider without thought changes its behaviour.

What assembly cannot do is calibrate. The trim and the accuracy statement belong to you or to a calibration lab, because both need references this floor does not hold.

### Where this floor stops, and it stops early here

This is the family where the list is longest, so it is worth being blunt:

- No cells and no pack. Balancing, state-of-charge accuracy and protection thresholds are proven by you; there is no BMS-against-a-real-pack test here.
- No grid-code or interconnection approval. UL 1741, VDE-AR-N 4105 or the local equivalent, plus anti-islanding: neither tested nor certified here.
- No system-level storage safety certification. UL 9540 / 9540A or its local equivalent is not held, not tested, and the fire test runs on a pack this floor never sees.
- No standby or sleep-current measurement. There is no microamp-level bench and no long-duration logging, so a self-consumption figure has to come from your own measurement.
- No pack-level or system-level end-of-line test, no ingress testing, no drop testing.

None of that makes the build worthless. It defines what you are buying: boards assembled and recorded to a drawing, not a storage system validated.

### Two hundred to two thousand, and a grid-code file that is not ours

The band is 200 to 2,000 pcs, which is high-mix territory: several boards, several variants, revision pressure from firmware and from certification. The practical advice is to keep the board count stable and put variant change in the BOM rather than in the layout, because a layout revision mid-certification restarts work you have already paid for.

For the cabinet-scale version of the same argument, including the high-voltage spacing question, see the rack BMS note (/insights/rack-bms-high-voltage-build-risk.html).

### What to send for a quote

Gerber with the stack-up and the isolation drawing, the BOM with the sense chain parts named, the centroid, the connector list with mating halves, the coating and mask list, and the quantity per board and per system. At 200 to 2,000 pcs a build is three working days from kitted parts.

The family page is residential and stackable storage boards (/applications/residential-storage.html). For the three-board question in a portable unit, should one assembler build all three power station boards (/insights/power-station-three-board-supplier.html).

## An induction board is judged at the pan, and the pan is the one thing this floor never connects

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/induction-tank-never-connected.html
Published: 2026-11-19
Summary: The resonant tank decides both the money and the failure, and it lives outside this building. Where an appliance drive build can be controlled, and where it cannot.

An induction hob board is a resonant inverter: a rectifier, an IGBT half-bridge, a resonant tank of capacitors and the coil, a control board and a display. One to three boards per appliance, a thousand to ten thousand pieces per order, and a market where a cent per board is a negotiation.

The reason this family deserves its own note is that its performance and its failure both live in the tank — and the tank is a coil of wire that is never connected on this floor.

### The resonant tank is where the money and the failure both are

The board's job is to switch an IGBT into a resonant circuit at the right moment, with the right dead time, and survive the commutation boundary. Everything hard about it is at that boundary:

- Commutation. If the switch is not soft at turn-on, losses and EMI spike together. That is a firmware and tank design problem, exercised at the pan.
- Resonant capacitors. They carry high ripple current and they are the parts that age. Where they sit, how their joints are formed, and how hot they run are all assembly-relevant.
- The IGBT's thermal path. Heavy copper, a heatsink or an aluminium substrate, and a joint whose voiding decides whether the device reaches its rated life.

So the honest position is: assembly controls the joints and the thermal path, the design controls the boundary, and only the appliance with a coil verifies the result. Which is why "we can build it, we cannot prove the tank" is the sentence to keep in mind at quotation time.

### Coating is not potting, and a kitchen is a wet room

Hobs get steamed, wiped, occasionally flooded. Conformal coating is applied here, with masking, and it does real work on the control side and the low-voltage areas.

It is not potting, and potting is not done here. The mains-side region usually relies on creepage, potting or a sealed enclosure, and the split has to be decided by whoever owns the appliance safety case. A board whose design assumes encapsulation is a board that needs a different supplier for the final step.

The other half of the wet argument is the glass panel and the seal, and neither is ours. Every leak complaint in this category is an enclosure discussion.

### What cannot be proven without a coil on the bench

Nothing below happens here, and each of them is a number a buyer needs:

- Output power, efficiency, temperature rise under load, and the commutation boundary — all need a resonant load and a coil plate.
- EMC pre-compliance and compliance testing — the hard gate for this family. Not something this floor can clear for you, and the reason designs get re-spun after first certification.
- Safety certification — CCC, CE, UL are granted to the appliance, not to the board.
- Potting and full encapsulation.
- Glass panel, coil plate, fan shroud and enclosure work.

If the acceptance plan needs any of those before a batch ships, they belong at the appliance maker or a test house, and the shipment plan should reflect that.

### One thousand to ten thousand, and a price fight

At 1,000 to 10,000 pcs the family is in a genuine price fight, and it is worth understanding what is actually being negotiated. On a board this simple, the visible variable is price and the invisible one is process stability — the argument made in the LED driver quote reality check (/insights/led-driver-quote-reality-check.html), which is the same market with the same dynamic.

Two levers that are real at this volume:

- Panel design and depanelisation. Long thin boards and heavy copper want a panel that carries them flat.
- One stencil, one profile, held across the year. The cheapest way to lose the cent you saved is a re-tooled batch that fails at the appliance line.

### Where this floor stops

- No resonant load, no coil plate — power, efficiency and commutation are unmeasured.
- No EMC testing of any kind.
- No appliance safety certification.
- No potting or encapsulation; coating is the only protection applied.
- No glass, coil, fan or enclosure assembly.

### What to send for a quote

Gerber with copper weights and the stack-up, the BOM with the IGBT and resonant capacitors named, the centroid, the heatsink or substrate interface, the coating and mask drawing, the connector and terminal list, and the quantity per variant. At 1,000 to 10,000 pcs a build is three working days from kitted parts.

The family page is induction and appliance inverter drives (/applications/induction-drive.html). For the same half-bridge at industrial margins, a VFD quoted as three boards or one set (/insights/vfd-three-boards-one-quote.html); for the quote that survives a second batch, the LED driver reality check (/insights/led-driver-quote-reality-check.html).

## An instrument board is fifty to five hundred pieces, and most of them are a revision

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/instrument-front-end-noise-floor.html
Published: 2026-11-19
Summary: Bench instruments are low volume, revision-heavy and analogue. What the assembly step decides about noise, and the calibration that never happens in this building.

A bench instrument is the kind of product where the buyer is an engineer who will notice a 2 µV offset and write about it. The boards are two or three: a front end, a control board, and a panel with the encoder and the display. Volumes are fifty to five hundred sets, and a good share of those orders are revisions rather than repeats.

That combination — low volume, high scrutiny, constant revision — decides what the supplier relationship has to look like, and it is not the same relationship that suits a consumer product.

### Small batches are the product, not a phase before volume

Instrument makers sometimes apologise for ordering fifty. There is nothing to apologise for: fifty pieces with four revisions a year is a normal instrument programme, and it is the shape this floor is built for. The cost structure is the one described in why fifty pieces cost more per board (/insights/fifty-piece-run-cost.html) — setup amortised over fifty, not over five thousand.

What makes it work is that the revisions are cheap. A stencil change and a re-profile on a fifty-piece run is a few hundred dollars; the same change on a five-thousand-piece run with tooling and test fixtures is a different conversation. A supplier who cannot do a fifty-piece revision economically will make you live with the design you have, which is worse for the instrument than the unit price is good.

### The front end is where assembly decides the noise floor

The analogue front end is a guarded, high-impedance, low-noise circuit, and the assembly contribution is decided by four things:

- Cleanliness. Residue across a guard ring is leakage, leakage is offset drift, and drift is a calibration failure six months later.
- Thermal symmetry. Two halves of a differential front end in different thermal environments read differently; the layout decides, but the reflow and the coating can make it worse.
- Coating callout. Coating over a sensitive divider changes its behaviour with humidity, sometimes for the better and sometimes for the worse — but never by accident.
- Relay and switch joints. Range switching relays and BNC sockets are through-hole and mechanically loaded, and they are the parts that get replaced in a service life measured in decades.

None of that appears on a placement report. All of it appears in a specification that says what is masked, what is washed, and how the joint is made.

### Relays, BNCs and the hand-work instruments still need

Instruments carry parts that no placer can handle: relays with large footprints, BNC and banana sockets, sometimes a rotary switch. Those are through-hole, often with a mechanical fixing to the panel, and the joint quality is inspected visually and by pull on the first article rather than by an AOI pass.

Where this matters is repeatability across revisions. If the through-hole work is redone by hand each time without a written method, revision three and revision five are different products that share a Gerber. That is the kind of drift that shows up as "the new batch doesn't match the reference unit".

### Calibration, accuracy and the parts that are not ours

The number on the datasheet is a metrology claim. It is produced by a calibration chain with references traceable to a national standard, and it does not exist in this building:

- No calibration, no accuracy or uncertainty statement.
- No in-circuit or functional test of the finished instrument.
- No EMC or safety qualification.
- No potting or full encapsulation of the front end. Coating is what this floor does.

What is delivered is boards assembled and recorded to a drawing, with first-article evidence and per-lot inspection data, so that your calibration step starts from a known build.

### What to send for a quote

Gerber with the stack-up, the BOM, the centroid, the through-hole parts list with the mechanical fixings, the coating and mask drawing with the guarded areas marked, and the quantity including the revision cadence if you want the reorder priced sensibly. At 50 to 500 sets a build is three working days from kitted parts.

The family page is test and measurement instrument boards (/applications/instruments.html). For why a reorder prices differently, why the second run costs less (/insights/why-the-second-run-costs-less.html), and for the DFM check that saves a stencil, what a DFM review catches (/insights/dfm-review-before-the-stencil.html).

## An IP camera board is easy to assemble and hard to prove, because the proof is an image

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/ip-camera-proof-is-an-image.html
Published: 2026-11-19
Summary: Five hundred to five thousand boards, a thermal SoC and an image-based acceptance criterion. Why the assembler's job is narrow and why the testing has to live somewhere else.

A security camera is a BGA SoC, a sensor connector, PoE magnetics, an IR cut filter driver and a lens — plus, on the access-control side, a small reader board with a keypad and a relay. The main board is a dense mixed-signal board with a thermally significant processor, and at 500 to 5,000 pieces it is squarely in the range a high-mix floor builds well.

The awkwardness is entirely in the acceptance criterion. A camera is judged by an image, and no image is produced in this building.

### The SoC is a thermal and a reflow problem at once

A camera SoC in a sealed dome is thermally constrained and electrically dense. Two consequences for the build:

- Voiding under the thermal pad. The SoC's ground pad is its heatsink. A void there raises the junction temperature in a housing with almost no airflow, and the symptom is a camera that drops frames in the afternoon rather than one that fails on the bench.
- Warpage and standoff. A large BGA on a board that also has a big sensor cutout and a gland hole is a board that wants to warp. Reflow profile and support during handling are the controls.

X-ray on the SoC is the inspection that matters, and it is worth receiving the images rather than a pass rate.

### PoE, connectors and the parts that get pulled

An Ethernet camera gets its power over the same pair it communicates on, and the port is the part most likely to be abused — by installers, by weather, by a cable that gets yanked.

- PoE magnetics and the isolation barrier need the creepage the drawing specifies, and assembly has to respect it through coating and mask decisions.
- The RJ45 or the gland is the mechanical interface. The board side of it takes strain, and a connector held only by solder joints is a repair waiting to happen.
- The IR LED ring and the light sensor are on the board but belong to the optics budget; position tolerance is set by the housing.

There is one part of the sealing story that is easy to misread: the gland seals the housing, not the board. Coating protects the board from condensation; it does not make the camera waterproof.

### What is not done here: the image, the protocol, the rating

Stated plainly, because this is the part buyers most often assume is included:

- No image tuning, lens focusing, IR-cut alignment, or any low-light, resolution or colour measurement.
- No functional test of any kind — no in-circuit test, no functional test, and no ONVIF or RTSP conformance work.
- No IP or IK testing, no salt-fog testing, no EMC pre-compliance or compliance testing.
- No potting of the camera module.

What is on offer is assembly, SPI, AOI, X-ray on the SoC and the power joints, coating with masking, and a lot record. If your acceptance plan assumes a picture is taken before shipping, that step is yours or your ODM's.

### Five hundred to five thousand, and the variants multiply

Cameras multiply variants faster than almost any family: lens options, IR or white light, PoE or 12 V, dome or bullet, reader or no reader. Each variant that changes the board is a new stencil-and-profile cycle; each variant that changes only the BOM is a changeover.

The discipline that keeps this affordable is deciding early which variants live in the BOM and which live in the layout — and then keeping the latter to as few as the market will allow. That is also the argument for keeping the reader board separate from the camera board rather than integrating them.

### What to send for a quote

Gerber with the stack-up, the BOM with the SoC and PoE magnetics named, the centroid, the sensor connector and gland drawing, the coating and mask drawing, the variant matrix, and the quantity. At 500 to 5,000 pcs a build is three working days from kitted parts.

The family page is IP cameras, NVR and access control boards (/applications/ip-camera.html). For the test-strategy question, what to do when your assembler has no in-circuit test (/insights/in-circuit-test-outsourcing.html); for how the record set is assembled on a safety-related board, the EVSE audit record set (/insights/evse-audit-record-set.html).

## On a receiver card the joint that fails is a ribbon header, three years later, on a wall nobody can reach

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/led-receiver-card-ribbon-headers.html
Published: 2026-11-19
Summary: A cabinet card is cheap, long, and covered in headers that get cycled during install. Why the connector and the through-hole fill decide the field failure, not the placement.

An LED display is a wall of identical cabinets, each with one or more receiver cards and a sender card upstream. The receiver card is long and narrow, usually with eight or more ribbon headers along its edge feeding hub boards, and it is ordered in thousands because the wall is measured in square metres.

The card is simple and cheap. That is exactly the problem: on a part this cheap, the only visible variable is price, and the only invisible variable is the process — which is why the failure this family produces is almost always the same one.

### Eight headers, and every one of them is a lever

A ribbon header is a mechanical interface that gets mated during installation, possibly re-mated during service, and then left for years. Three things about it are decided at build:

- Through-hole fill. These are through-hole parts on a thin board. Insufficient fill gives a joint that survives the factory and cracks on the third installation.
- Header seating and coplanarity. A header that is a fraction off-square puts the ribbon under tension, and the tension lands on the solder joints at both ends.
- Handing during packing. Long thin boards flex. A card that is packed with the headers taking the load arrives pre-stressed.

An AOI pass rate says nothing about any of those three. A pull test on the first article and a written seating method do.

### This family is priced in cents and ordered in thousands

At 1,000 to 10,000 pcs, the economics are dominated by material and yield, not by setup. Which changes the honest advice: the lever here is not negotiation, it is the panel design and the process stability.

- Panelisation matters more than on any other family. Long boards with a high header count want a panel that carries them flat through reflow and depanelisation.
- One stencil revision, held. A card that is re-tooled between batches at this price point is a batch that will differ.
- Coating, if specified, is a cost you should interrogate. Outdoor cabinets usually want it; indoor rental walls often do not. Coating eight headers correctly means masking eight headers, and that labour is real.

The cent-per-board argument is worth reading before you buy on price: how to tell whether an LED driver quote is real (/insights/led-driver-quote-reality-check.html) makes the same case one step upstream in the same industry.

### What is not measured here: the colour, the wall, the EMC

Nothing on this floor produces a picture. Specifically not available:

- Colour, brightness, gamma or refresh calibration at cabinet level, and any pixel-level or wall-level test.
- EMC pre-compliance or compliance testing, ingress (IP) testing, salt-fog and UV ageing of the cabinet.
- Cabinet mechanical assembly, power-supply integration, front-face lamination.
- Any end-to-end proof that the finished screen works before it ships.

So the acceptance plan is yours: a test jig on the hub interface, a burn-in rack, and a cabinet-level visual check at the integrator. That is normal for this industry — but it means the assembler is being bought for consistency, not for proof.

### Where the board stops and somebody else starts

A clean split looks like this: the card is assembled, inspected, and recorded here; the cabinet is built, powered, sealed and calibrated by the cabinet maker; the wall is commissioned on site with the control system. Almost every dispute in this product category comes from one of those three steps being assumed by the wrong party.

### What to send for a quote

Gerber with the panelisation, the stack-up, the BOM, the centroid, the header list with the seating and pull requirements, the coating and mask drawing if any, and the quantity with the variant count. At 1,000 to 10,000 pcs the build is three working days from kitted parts, and the through-hole operation is the rate limiter.

The family page is LED display control and receiver cards (/applications/led-display.html). For the coating-versus-cost argument in this industry, the LED driver quote reality check (/insights/led-driver-quote-reality-check.html); for where a cheap board stops being cheap, what is inside a PCBA price (/insights/pcba-cost-per-board.html).

## On a medical device the board is ordinary and the record is not

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/medical-board-ordinary-record-is-not.html
Published: 2026-11-19
Summary: Acquisition, main and UI boards in a device that lives a decade. Why the assembly question is about documents and revisions rather than about placement.

Of all the families on this site, medical is the one where the assembly is least interesting and the paperwork is most. A patient monitor or a diagnostic instrument carries two or three boards: an acquisition board with a guarded analogue front end, a main board, and a UI or panel board. Fine pitch, sometimes BGA, sometimes a guarded ring on the analogue side. Most competent lines can build it.

What most lines cannot do is answer a question two years later about which lot a serial came from, and that is the question a medical programme is actually buying.

### What this floor can be to a device maker

The honest description is: a competent contract assembler with ISO 9001:2015, working to your drawings, with a per-lot record you can retrieve. That is a real and useful role for a device company that owns its design, its firmware, its clinical validation and its regulatory submission.

What it is not is a medical-certified manufacturer. ISO 13485 is not held here, and neither is the quality-system audit trail that comes with it. A device that needs its contract manufacturer inside the QMS scope needs a different counterpart, and finding that out during an audit is expensive.

### Cleanliness and guarding: where assembly changes the reading

The analogue front end on an acquisition board is guarded for a reason, and three assembly habits quietly defeat the guard:

- Flux and residue across the guard ring. No-clean processes are fine when they are consistently no-clean; a repair with activated flux that is never washed is not.
- Coating bridging a guarded area. The mask list is not optional on this family. Coat the ring and the leakage number moves.
- Handling. Boards that sit open on a bench pick up what the room contains, and this family is low volume, so they sit longer.

None of those shows up as a failure at inspection. They show up as a channel that drifts, and then as a service visit.

### A lot record that survives a question two years later

The record set worth agreeing in writing, because it is what a medical customer asks for:

- First-article photographs and the drawing revision they were built to
- SPI results before reflow and AOI results after, filed per lot rather than summarised
- X-ray images for BGA and any guarded-joint area, per lot
- The coating record with the mask list used
- Traceability from lot to the component date codes that went in

A record that exists is worth a great deal in a complaint. A record that was summarised into a pass percentage is worth nothing, because it cannot answer the only question being asked.

### A device lives for a decade; the BOM does not

Medical instruments stay in service far longer than the parts inside them stay in production. The substitution question therefore arrives on every programme sooner or later, and it needs a written process rather than a phone call: who may propose an alternate, what evidence comes with it, who signs, and whether the change requires re-verification on your side.

That process is worth more than a lower unit price, and it is the point where a supplier who is honest about lifecycle becomes cheaper than one who is simply cheap.

### Where this floor stops

- ISO 13485 certification and any QMS audit trail under it. Not held.
- Sterilisation, biocompatibility and packaging validation, and the regulatory submission itself.
- In-circuit or functional test of the finished device, and any test that touches patient safety.
- Volumes in the tens of thousands a year, where a medical-certified contract manufacturer is the right counterpart.

### What to send for a quote

Gerber with the stack-up and the guarding drawing, the BOM, the centroid, the coating and mask list including guarded areas, the record set you require, the substitution policy you want followed, and the quantity. At 100 to 1,000 sets the build is three working days from kitted parts.

The family page is medical device and diagnostic instrument boards (/applications/medical.html). For the same argument applied to another certified industry, do you need IATF 16949 for an aftermarket part (/insights/no-iatf-16949.html); for what inspection actually proves, what AOI and X-ray can and cannot catch (/insights/what-aoi-xray-cannot-catch.html).

## An off-highway controller is judged in a field six months after it left the line

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/off-highway-coating-in-a-casting.html
Published: 2026-11-19
Summary: One or two boards per machine, coated, with valve drivers on the logic side and load dump on the power side. Where the build risk sits before the machine is ever driven.

A tractor or excavator controller is one or two boards inside a sealed cast aluminium housing bolted to a frame. It drives hydraulic valve solenoids, reads sensors, talks over CAN, and lives in dust, vibration, and a temperature range that a sealed casting makes worse rather than better.

It is also the family where the gap between what assembly can prove and what the machine will experience is widest. That gap is not a defect; it is a boundary, and buyers who know where it sits make better decisions about price.

### Coating is not a finish on this family, it is the product

Every board here is conformal coated, and the coating is doing real work: condensation, dust, oil mist and the occasional pressure wash nearby.

What that requires is a specification rather than a bottle:

- Mask list. Sealed connector pins, test points, pressure-sensitive sensors, and any surface that must stay conductive. A coated connector pin is a fault that appears as a communication error on a cold morning.
- Material and thickness. Polyurethane and silicone behave differently on thermal cycling; the callout should name one and say how the film is checked.
- Cure before handling. Coated boards that are handled wet lose the coating exactly where the harness lands.
- Rework sequence. Cut back, repair, re-coat, and record it. A reworked board without re-coating is a board with a hole in its protection.

The rest of the family follows from this: a coated board forces you to think about what is masked, and what is masked forces you to think about what the housing has to seal.

### Valve current, load dump, and the joints that carry both

The power side is heavy copper driving inductive loads, and the failure modes are the classic ones:

Risk: Where it is decided · What inspection proves
Voiding under the FETs: Paste volume, reflow profile · X-ray on the power joints, per lot
Solder fill on valve driver tabs: Through-hole method, thermal mass · First-article pull and cross-section
Coating bridging the isolation gap: Mask drawing, coating method · Visual under magnification, photographed
Connector strain: Connector choice, board edge design · Nothing — it is a design decision

That last row is the honest one. Some of the most important decisions on this family cannot be inspected at all, because they were made on the drawing.

### What is not proven here: sealing, EMC, vibration, functional safety

The list is long and it is worth stating without softening:

- No ingress (IP) testing, no burst or leak-down test of the sealed casting, and therefore no IP rating for the finished controller.
- No EMC, load-dump, vibration, thermal-shock or salt-spray qualification, and no certified test report.
- No functional safety certification — ISO 13849, IEC 61508, any PL or SIL claim — and no IATF 16949 work as a Tier supplier.
- No hydraulic valve calibration or end-of-line actuator test.
- No potting or encapsulation of the board. Coating is what this floor does.

A machine programme that needs any of those is not being badly served by this floor; it is being served by the wrong party for those steps, which is a different and more fixable problem.

### A hundred machines is a normal order, and it stays a hundred

At 100 to 1,000 sets, this is a long-life, low-volume, revision-light family — the opposite of a consumer product. The right supplier is one whose process does not drift between orders two years apart, and whose record lets you prove it did not.

That is why the useful question at quotation is not "what is your price at 500" but "what does your record look like, and can I have the first-article pack from the last time you built this".

### What to send for a quote

Gerber with copper weights and the stack-up, the BOM including the load-dump and protection parts, the centroid, the sealed connector list with the mating half and pin assignment, the coating and mask drawing with the isolation gap marked, the valve driver joint callout, and the quantity. At 100 to 1,000 sets a build is three working days from kitted parts.

The family page is off-highway and agricultural controllers (/applications/off-highway.html). For the similar coating argument in a handheld, where the coating is the product (/insights/rugged-radio-coating-is-the-product.html); for the certification question in automotive work, do you need IATF 16949 (/insights/no-iatf-16949.html).

## A payment terminal has one trace that must never be nicked, and nothing here can prove it survived

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/payment-terminal-tamper-mesh.html
Published: 2026-11-19
Summary: Two to four boards per terminal, one of them wrapped in a mesh whose failure is silent. Why the audit should come before the price, and who owns provisioning.

A payment terminal is two to four boards: a main board, a keypad and reader board, a printer board, sometimes a display board. On the main board there is a tamper detection mesh — a fine, dense, deliberate pattern of traces whose whole purpose is to break in a way the secure element can detect.

That mesh turns an ordinary assembly job into one with a single catastrophic failure mode that leaves no symptom at inspection. Which is why the security conversation belongs at the start of the programme rather than in the last week before certification.

### Start with the audit, because the buyer will

A terminal buyer eventually gets audited, and the audit reaches the manufacturing chain. What it looks for is not a claim of capability but evidence of control: who handled the boards, what the process was, what records exist, and what happens when a board fails.

Two things are true and both need saying early:

- This floor is not inside a payment-security certification. No PCI PTS approval, no EMVCo test report, no scheme audit, no secure facility.
- This floor can build and record boards to a drawing, including the mesh as an assembly feature, with per-lot traceability.

A programme that needs its manufacturer inside the security scope needs a different counterpart. A programme that needs boards built and recorded, with security verification on your side, is a fit — provided that split is agreed in writing.

### The tamper mesh is an assembly feature before it is a security feature

The mesh is inspected as a physical feature here: continuity of the pattern, no scratch, no solder splash, no coating bridging two traces that must stay separate.

Three process realities:

- Coating over a mesh is a decision, not a default. Coating can protect the mesh mechanically; it can also hide a bridge until the secure element reports tampering, at which point the unit is scrap.
- Rework near the mesh is close to forbidden. A board that needs rework inside the mesh area is usually a board that should be scrapped, and the process should say so rather than leaving it to judgement at the station.
- Handling. A dense fine-pitch board with a mesh on it does not want to be stacked, slid or squeezed, and at 500 to 5,000 pieces there are plenty of opportunities.

Continuity testing of the mesh is yours. This floor can inspect it as a feature and photograph it; it cannot tell you whether the detection circuit behaves.

### Secure-element provisioning and key injection

The question that stops programmes is who holds the key material. It is not a manufacturing preference; it is a security architecture decision with a certificate attached.

The rule that works: decide it in writing before the first build, never add it mid-run. If key injection happens at a party that holds the key material, the boards ship uninjected and the process after that belongs to them. If it happens here, the process, the environment and the audit trail all have to be agreed first — and this floor does not provision secure elements as a standard build step.

The same reasoning applies to card-reader function: magstripe, contact and contactless reads are not exercised here. There is no in-circuit test and no functional test, so the first time a card is tapped is at your bench. That is workable; assuming otherwise is not.

### The parts that get abused: printer, keypad, card slot

Terminals are handled by the public, all day. The board-level consequences are mechanical:

- Keypad and reader board joints take repeated force; through-hole and reinforced pads are drawing decisions.
- The card slot is a lever into the housing; the board behind it should not be the thing limiting insertion depth.
- The printer assembly is the highest-cycle mechanism in the product and is usually its own board for exactly that reason.

### Where this floor stops

- Tamper-mesh continuity, tamper response and key destruction. Verified by you with the secure element in place.
- Any payment-scheme approval or test, and any secure facility.
- Secure-element provisioning and key injection as a standard step.
- Card-reader function of any kind, and any in-circuit or functional test.
- Drop, ingress and EMC testing, and sitting inside the security certification scope.

### What to send for a quote

Gerber with the stack-up, the BOM with the secure element named, the centroid, the mesh drawing and the mask list, the keypad and reader connector list, the printer interface, and the quantity plus the variant matrix. At 500 to 5,000 pcs a build is three working days from kitted parts.

The family page is POS and payment terminal boards (/applications/pos-terminal.html). For how the manufacturing audit actually runs, how to audit a PCBA supplier without visiting (/insights/pcba-supplier-audit-checklist.html); for the test question, what to do when your assembler has no in-circuit test (/insights/in-circuit-test-outsourcing.html).

---

## The motor tabs on a power tool controller are soldered, and that is the whole job

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/power-tool-motor-tabs-soldered.html
Published: 2026-11-19
Summary: One or two boards, thousands of identical pieces, and a joint carrying twenty amps inside a sealed handle. Why the through-hole tabs and the coating decide field life.

A brushless tool controller is a power board that lives inside a handle. No fan, no airflow, no service access, and a user who will run it until the battery is flat and then put it down hot. The circuit is a three-phase bridge, a gate driver, current sense and a microcontroller that reads a trigger. Simple.

What is not simple is that the board's two hardest joints are the ones carrying the motor current, and they are made by hand or by selective solder rather than by the placer. On a tool, the assembly's job is those joints, the coating, and the fact that there are five thousand of them.

### A power board, not a computing board

Two or three ounces of copper on the power side, a heavy-copper bridge under a heatsink or a potted block, and a control section that could fit on a fingernail. Everything about the build follows from that split:

- The bridge needs a documented reflow profile. Heavy copper on one side and fine traces on the other is a compromise, and a profile borrowed from another board is a latent void.
- Voiding under the FETs is the yield number. Not the placement count, not the AOI pass rate. A voided joint on a 20 A bridge is a device that runs hot and derates in the user's hand.
- The heatsink interface is mechanical. Pad or paste, flatness, and the torque on the mounting screws. All three belong on the drawing.

### The motor tabs are soldered, not placed

The motor connects to the board through tabs or a terminal block, and that joint carries the full phase current. It is through-hole, it is thermally massive, and it is done in-house here by selective or hand solder with the joint specified and inspected.

Three failure modes are worth naming because none of them shows up on an AOI screen:

- Insufficient fill. Looks soldered, measures cold, heats under load, fails in month four.
- Cold joint on a plated tab. No amount of flux fixes a surface that will not wet; it needs the plating and the paste to be compatible.
- Mechanical load applied to the joint. If the tab is also the mounting point, the solder is taking vibration, and the drawing should say what takes it instead.

This is the single reason a tool controller is not a commodity assembly: the joints that decide the warranty are the ones a placer never touches.

### Coating, and the housing that is not ours

Most tool controllers are coated, because a tool gets rained on and put down in wet grass. It is applied here with connectors and the battery contacts masked.

Two things coating is not: it is not potting, and it is not the housing seal. Potting is not done here, and closing the handle around the board is the tool brand's operation. A design that relies on the coating for water ingress is asking it to do a job it was not specified for — the same argument as on a storage board, at a much lower voltage.

### Batch size, and why the volume argument turns early

A tool programme is usually 1,000 to 5,000 sets, and above roughly 10,000 sets a month a dedicated high-volume line wins on unit price honestly. The reason is not mystery: at that volume the line is set once and run, and changeover stops being a share of the unit cost.

Between those two points, a high-mix floor is the right counterpart, and the thing that decides your price is not the placement count but how many variants you have. A single controller in three firmware variants is one build; three power levels with different bridges is three.

### Where this floor stops

- Motor, gearbox and switch test under load. A dynamometer or torque rig belongs at the tool brand's end-of-line station.
- Potting, overmoulding and closing the housing around the board.
- Tool-level safety or regulatory testing — the certification belongs to the finished tool.
- Volumes above roughly 10,000 sets a month, where a dedicated line wins.

### What to send for a quote

Gerber with copper weights per layer, the stack-up, the BOM with the FETs named by package, the motor tab and terminal drawing with the joint called out, the heatsink interface and torque, the coating and mask list, and the quantity per variant. At 1,000 to 5,000 sets a build is three working days from kitted parts.

The family page is brushless power tool controllers (/applications/power-tool.html). For how the unit price is actually built up, see what is inside a PCBA price (/insights/pcba-cost-per-board.html), and for the inspection argument, what AOI and X-ray can and cannot catch (/insights/what-aoi-xray-cannot-catch.html).
