## What to do when your PCBA supplier does not run in-circuit test

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/in-circuit-test-outsourcing.html
Published: 2026-11-17
Summary: Outsourcing the test step is workable if the fixture, the program and the per-serial record are all specified in writing. What you lose is same-day feedback; what you must never accept is a visual check standing in for electrical proof.

If your assembler does not run in-circuit test, the fixture still has to exist somewhere. The workable arrangement is a test partner who builds the fixture, runs the program and reports per serial number, managed by the assembler as one line on the quote. What you lose is same-day feedback. What you keep is a documented electrical record. What you must not accept is "we check it visually" standing in for electrical proof.

### Why ICT decides which assemblers can even quote

Two plants with identical placement equipment are not interchangeable the moment your BOM requires electrical test. In-circuit test needs a bed-of-nails fixture, a program derived from your netlist, and a tester — capital and engineering that a placement-focused plant often does not carry.

So the honest first question is not "how good are your lines" but "who owns my test step". If the answer is "nobody, we just don't do it", you are not buying an assembly service, you are buying half of one.

### Three arrangements, and what each one actually costs you

Arrangement: What it looks like · You gain · You lose
In-house ICT at the assembler: Fixture and program built and run on the same site · Same-day feedback, one PO, one schedule · Higher unit price; smaller plants rarely offer it
Partner test, managed by the assembler: Fixture built by a qualified test house, run there, results returned per serial, quoted as its own line · One commercial contact; test record still documented; assembly keeps its 50-piece minimum · Boards travel once more; feedback is hours-to-a-day, not immediate
Test at your own plant or your ODM: Boards ship untested electrically · Full control of test coverage and data · You carry freight, re-test logistics and the cost of catching defects late

There is no fourth option. A visual-only release is not a test arrangement; it is an absence.

### How to specify the partner arrangement in a purchase order

When the test step is outsourced, the risk moves into the wording. Four clauses make the difference:

- Fixture ownership. State who owns the fixture and where it is stored. Owning it yourself is what makes a second source possible later.
- Program source. The test program derives from your netlist. Require it delivered to you, with the revision it was built against.
- Record format. Results per serial, not a pass/fail count. Ask for the columns before the first lot, not after.
- Failure handling. What happens to a board that fails — reworked how, logged where, re-tested by whom. A batch-level "reworked" note is not a record.

### What records to demand

For each lot, four documents. If any is missing, the test did not happen in any auditable sense:

- First-article result with the fixture ID and program revision
- Per-serial results file for the full lot
- Failure log with the disposition of every failed board
- The calibration status of the tester used, dated inside the lot window

### When ICT is genuinely unnecessary

ICT is not a virtue in itself. It is worth its cost when a fault is expensive to find later and cheap to find now.

- Skip it when the board is simple, the batch is small, and a functional check at your own bench catches what matters. A 50-piece run of a keypad board rarely justifies a fixture.
- Skip it when your product's real pass criteria live in firmware and mechanics, not in net continuity. A VFD is the clearest case: the drive's load test belongs with the drive builder, whose firmware defines pass and fail.
- Never skip it when the board is dense, double-sided, 01005 with 0.3 mm pitch, and the failure mode is an intermittent that only shows up in the field. On a robot vacuum mainboard, ICT is usually the requirement that decides which assemblers can quote at all.

That last point is why our own capability page states plainly that in-circuit and functional test are not run in-house. It costs us enquiries from buyers who need one roof. It saves the ones who would have found out at the tooling stage.

### What we do instead, here

Solder joints are covered inside the building: in-line 3D SPI before placement, AOI after reflow on every board, X-ray on BGA, QFN and power-device joints read by an operator rather than a green light, with images filed against the lot. Thickness, warpage and finish are checked on incoming bare boards. Every first article is photographed and filed.

What is not covered inside the building is electrical proof of function. That runs through a qualified test partner, coordinated by us, quoted as a separate line. We say so at quotation, not at shipment.

Table 03 on capabilities.html (/capabilities.html) lists what each inspection step proves and where it stops. For the general shape of the problem, what AOI and X-ray still cannot catch (/insights/what-aoi-xray-cannot-catch.html) is the companion note.

## Where liability sits on a jump starter with an air compressor

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/jump-starter-safety-liability.html
Published: 2026-11-17
Summary: A jump starter can destroy a vehicle's electronics if one switch fails. That risk has to be allocated in the paperwork, not assumed from a good build.

A jump starter with an integrated air compressor is two boards: a main board carrying the high-current MOSFET switch and the battery management, and a compressor drive board. Assembly is not the hard part. The hard part is that this product connects a lithium pack to somebody's vehicle electronics through a switch you built.

### The failure that matters is not a solder joint

If the high-current switch fails closed, the vehicle sees the jump pack's voltage at full current with no control. That is not a warranty event on a small appliance; it is damage to an ECU. Every other risk in this product is smaller than that one.

Which means the sourcing conversation is not primarily about placement capability. It is about the specification the board was built to, the evidence that the build matched it, and the written allocation of what happens if it does not.

### The two boards are not equally risky

Board: What it carries · Process risk · Commercial risk
Main: MOSFET switch, BMS front end, protection comparators, reverse-polarity path · High-current joints, heat, through-hole terminals · The liability board
Compressor drive: Motor drive, pressure sensing input · Moderate current, simpler layout · Lower — a failure stops the compressor

Both are built in the 100 sets to 1,000 sets band, and both are usually conformally coated because the unit lives in a car boot and gets damp. The main board is where the through-hole terminals and the high-current path live, and those joints carry current and mechanical load at once.

### What an assembler can and cannot certify

This boundary needs to be explicit, because buyers frequently assume more than an assembly house can offer.

Item: Who owns it
Placement, reflow, coating, through-hole joints: Assembler
Conformance to an assembly standard (IPC-A-610 class as specified): Assembler
X-ray of the MOSFET and high-current joints: Assembler, if specified
Cell-level safety of the battery pack: Cell supplier and pack assembler
Reverse-polarity and over-current behaviour of the product: Brand's design, verified by the brand's test
Product certification and market access: Brand owner
Field liability: Whoever the contract says — so write it

None of that is evasive. It is simply that an assembly house builds a board to a drawing; it does not certify a product's safety behaviour. A supplier who implies otherwise is the one to be careful with.

### The high-current joints are the assembly-side control

The switch and its terminals are where a build defect becomes a safety event. Two things are worth specifying:

- X-ray on the MOSFET and the high-current terminals, not just AOI. A void under a power device is invisible from the surface, and it is what turns a marginal joint into a hot spot.
- Through-hole fill criteria stated on the drawing. A terminal pin wetted on one side passes continuity and heats under load. Say what fill percentage and what hole fill is acceptable, and say whether it is inspected by cross-section or by X-ray.

Coating comes after that, and the coating mask has to leave the terminals and the clamp contact area clear. On a damp-boot product, a coated terminal is a bad connection waiting to happen.

### What the reverse-polarity path changes

Most jump starters include protection against connecting the clamps backwards. That path involves either a relay, a MOSFET arrangement, or a fuse-and-diode scheme, and every version of it has a component that must fail safely.

Ask for the DFM note on that specific path. Not because the assembler designed it, but because if the protection depends on a part that is hard to solder or a thermal pad that needs voiding control, that has to be known before the stencil is cut rather than after a batch is built.

### What to put in the enquiry

- Gerber, BOM and centroid for both boards, plus the stack-up for the main board.
- The current rating and duration of the jump path, since that sets the copper and the joint criteria.
- The X-ray requirement, named per component rather than as "standard inspection".
- Through-hole fill criteria and the inspection method.
- Coating mask zones — terminals and clamp contacts stay clear.
- Whether the unit is shipped with the battery installed, because that changes packing, transport classification and the final inspection step.

The jump starter page (/applications/jump-starter.html) states the two-board split, the high-current switch and terminal arrangement and the batch band. The e-bike controller (/applications/ebike.html) carries the same heavy-current-beside-logic problem with a potting mask on top, and the LED driver (/applications/led-driver.html) is the other family where a through-hole joint is the classic field failure. What AOI and X-ray cannot catch (/insights/what-aoi-xray-cannot-catch.html) explains why the high-current joints need the X-ray rather than the camera.

The build is ordinary. The allocation of risk is not — write it down before the first batch, not after the first claim.

On an unchanged revision the standard build here is 3 days from kitted parts, which is the number to plan a reorder against rather than a promise about component lead time.

Last reviewed: 2026-11-17 · Discuss a high-current board build: WhatsApp (https://wa.me/8617361058693)

## How to tell whether an LED driver PCBA quote is real

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/led-driver-quote-reality-check.html
Published: 2026-11-17
Summary: On a simple board everyone can quote, the price is the only visible variable — which is exactly why the invisible process steps decide who is cheaper in year two.

An LED driver and a USB-C fast charger are the same board in different clothes: an AC-DC front end, a power-factor stage and a regulated output, inside a sealed enclosure nobody opens. The board is simple enough that a dozen shops can quote it, the volume is enormous, and buyers switch over fractions of a cent. That makes it the family where quote quality matters most and is checked least.

### Why the cheapest quote is usually comparing different products

On a dense fine-pitch board, a low quote is suspicious because the capability is visible. On a driver board, capability is not the differentiator — anyone can place it. What differs is what is included around the placement, and that is where the cheap quote and the expensive quote stop describing the same thing.

Five items account for most of the gap:

Line item: What "not included" looks like · How it shows up later
Through-hole magnetics: Quoted as a placement job; transformer pins flow-soldered on one side · Pin wetted on one side passes continuity, heats in service
Cleaning before coating: Coating applied over unwashed flux · Isolation degrades; failures appear in humid installations only
Coating mask and thickness: "Fully coated" with no keep-clear drawing · Barrier bridged at the optocoupler or the isolation slot
Potting fill and voiding: Potting quoted by weight, not by fill depth · Case temperature marginal; units fail in a sealed enclosure
Isolation test at first article: Optical inspection only · The creepage the layout specified was never verified

None of these are exotic. They are simply the steps a supplier removes to reach a number, and they are exactly the steps that decide whether a driver survives five years in a streetlight.

### The through-hole problem is the honest one

Transformers, inductors and the input fuse are through-hole parts with real mass. A transformer pin carries current and mechanical load at the same time. Selective or wave soldering handles most of it; hand work fills in where a nozzle cannot reach.

Ask which soldering process is used, not what the price is. A quote that assumes wave soldering on the whole board and a quote that assumes hand soldering of the magnetics are different products. On a driver at 1,000 sets to 10,000 sets, the difference is visible in the second batch, when a few percent come back for a hot transformer.

### Thermal is a potting decision, not a layout decision

A driver runs inside a sealed enclosure with no fan. The switching devices and the transformer dissipate into the board and into the potting compound. Fill depth and voiding are therefore functional parameters.

The trap is that a unit which was fine on a bench in still air can be marginal once potted, if the compound was chosen for cost rather than conductivity. That choice belongs to the buyer, but it has to be raised before the batch rather than after — because once a unit is potted, the board inside it is not inspectable and not reworkable.

### Where this family stops being a good idea

Be clear about the commercial shape. A thousand to ten thousand pieces, enormous volume, thin margin, a board a dozen shops can build. Buyers switch on fractions of a cent. This is capacity filler for a high-mix floor, not a route to a durable relationship.

If the decision is purely unit price at high monthly volume, a dedicated high-volume plant beats a mixed-production floor, and it is fairer to say so than to win the order and lose it at the next re-quote. The reason to build it on a high-mix floor is different: small batches of several SKUs, long-tail variants, or a driver that ships inside a bigger product and has to match its change cadence.

### What to put in the enquiry

- Gerber, BOM and centroid, plus the isolation slot geometry marked on the drawing.
- The soldering method expected for the magnetics — this one question separates most of the field.
- Coating material, thickness, and the keep-clear zones. A named material is better than "conformal coating".
- Whether the unit is potted, and to what fill depth.
- The workload shape, not just the annual volume: how many SKUs, how often they change. That is what a high-mix floor prices well and a volume plant prices badly.

The LED driver and PD charger page (/applications/led-driver.html) states the batch band and says outright that a dedicated high-volume plant wins above ten thousand pieces a month. The parking sensor board (/applications/parking-sensor.html) is the other family here where potting happens before the board can be tested, and the power station inverter (/applications/power-station.html) shares the sealed-enclosure thermal argument. Consigned versus turnkey PCBA (/insights/consigned-vs-turnkey-pcba.html) matters on this family more than most, because magnetics and electrolytics are where material price moves.

A driver quote is a process statement with a number attached. Read the process first.

On an unchanged revision the standard build here is 3 days from kitted parts, which is the number to plan a reorder against rather than a promise about component lead time.

Last reviewed: 2026-11-17 · Ask for a driver quote with the process shown: WhatsApp (https://wa.me/8617361058693)

## Do you need IATF 16949 for an automotive aftermarket part?

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/no-iatf-16949.html
Published: 2026-11-17
Summary: A 12 V retail accessory is a consumer product and does not need IATF 16949. A replacement part sold into the vehicle service chain increasingly does. The difference decides whether the certificate is a requirement or paperwork.

IATF 16949 applies to sites that manufacture production, service or accessory parts for vehicle manufacturers. A 12 V accessory sold at retail — a jump starter, a dashcam, a parking sensor — is a consumer product and does not require it. We do not hold IATF 16949, and for aftermarket 12 V work that is not a gap. It becomes a gap the moment your board carries a PPAP obligation inside a vehicle programme.

### What IATF 16949 actually covers

IATF 16949 is a quality management system standard for automotive production and relevant service parts. It is written for sites — a plant, an address, a scope — not for a company in the abstract. The certificate names the site and the scope, and work outside that scope is not certified even if the same company performs it.

Two consequences that matter at quotation stage:

- A certificate whose holder name differs from the company you are paying does not automatically certify your supplier. Check the holder, the address and the scope, in that order.
- A certificate for bare-board fabrication does not cover assembly. If your supplier fabricates and does not assemble, the certificate says nothing about the step you are buying.

### Where a 12 V retail accessory sits

The dividing line is not "car-related" or "not car-related". It is whether the part is built to a vehicle manufacturer's specification and enters their production or service chain.

Product: Built to OEM spec? · Enters OEM chain? · IATF 16949 expected?
Control board inside a new vehicle: Yes · Yes · Yes — supplier is inside the chain
Replacement module sold for vehicle repair: Often yes · Yes, as a service part · Increasingly yes — see the note below
12 V jump starter sold in retail: No · No · No
Dashcam, parking sensor, LED headlight driver sold as accessories: No · No · No
EVSE control board for a charging point: Depends on the buyer · Depends · Check with the buyer, not with us

A note on aftermarket replacement parts. The scheme rules moved. IATF's Rules 6th Edition, published in December 2024, confirmed that organisations producing parts that replace original parts on a vehicle are eligible for IATF 16949 certification, and certification-body guidance since then states that those aftermarket processes must be fully inside the certification scope by 1 January 2028. If your product is a replacement part for vehicle repair rather than a retail accessory that never gets installed on a vehicle, treat this as a live question and confirm the current position with your customer and your certification body. This page explains scope; it is not legal advice and it is not a substitute for the standard itself.

### Three questions that tell you which side you are on

- Does your customer name IATF 16949 in the purchase order? If yes, the decision is already made — you need a supplier who holds it, whatever the technical merit.
- Is your board's failure mode a vehicle safety event, or a disappointed end user? A jump starter that fails is a return. A brake controller that fails is a recall. The paperwork follows the consequence.
- Will a vehicle manufacturer or a Tier 1 ever audit the plant that builds your board? If nobody upstream will ever ask for PPAP, the certification is buying you a document nobody requests.

Answer all three "no" and you are outside the scope that matters, whatever the product category suggests.

### What we hold, and what we do not

Item: Status · What it means in practice
ISO 9001: Held — certificate 38822Q00487R0S (38822Q00487R0S), scope: processing and assembly of digital electronics · Quality system audited at the plant
IATF 16949: Not held · We are not a Tier supplier inside a vehicle programme
ISO 13485: Not held · Medical device validation is not supported
Third-party IPC Class 3: Not held · Workmanship follows IPC-A-610 at the class agreed on the order
In-house ICT / FCT: Not available · Fixtures and programs run through a qualified test partner
Bare-board fabrication: Not available · Boards come from partner fabs, inspected on arrival

The ISO certificate is issued to Shenzhen Tengmei Technology Co., Ltd., which is the pinyin romanisation of the registered Chinese name of the entity trading as TENMAY. The unified social credit code 91440300670000384N resolves the link without relying on the spelling of the English name.

### What to ask a supplier who claims IATF 16949

Four questions, in this order, and ask for documents rather than assurances:

- Who is the certificate holder, exactly? Compare it with the entity on your proforma invoice. Different names are the single most common finding.
- What is the scope wording? "Manufacture of printed circuit boards" and "assembly of electronic assemblies" are different scopes.
- Which site does it cover? A group certificate and a plant address are not the same thing.
- Is it current, and who accredited the body? Ask for the certificate PDF and check the expiry and the accreditation mark.

A supplier who answers all four in writing within a day is either certified or well organised. A supplier who sends a photo of a framed certificate has told you nothing.

### When to walk away from us

Say it plainly, because it saves both sides a month:

- Your programme requires PPAP submission and a supplier registered to IATF 16949 → we are the wrong plant, and we will say so at quotation rather than after tooling.
- Your device needs ISO 13485 validation → same answer.
- Your board needs in-circuit and functional test at the assembler, with same-day feedback → we coordinate test through a partner; if you need it under one roof, choose a plant that runs it in-house.

What we do have is an assembly floor sized for 50 to 5,000 pieces: eight Yamaha YSM20/YSM10 lines, 01005 to 0.30 mm pitch, 800 × 480 mm boards, in-line SPI, AOI and X-ray, conformal coating, through-hole and box build in one building, three working days from kitted parts.

The same boundary list, written as a table you can check, is on company.html (/company.html). The process limits behind those numbers are on capabilities.html (/capabilities.html).

## Potting before test turns a defect into scrap

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/parking-sensor-potting-before-test.html
Published: 2026-11-17
Summary: The board is cheap and the potting is irreversible. Sequence the test before the encapsulation and a defect costs one board; sequence it after and it costs the unit.

A parking sensor control board is small, heavily panelised, and almost always conformally coated or potted, because it lives behind a bumper and sees water, salt and stone chips. Nothing about the board is difficult. The decision that matters is the order of the last two operations.

### The irreversible step

Coating is reversible in principle — it can be stripped, with effort and some risk to the board. Potting is not. Once the compound cures, the board inside it is not inspectable, not reworkable and not repairable. A defect that would have been a two-minute rework becomes a scrapped unit with the compound, the housing and the labour already spent.

That means the test coverage question is not "how much testing do we want". It is "what must be proven before the point of no return".

Stage: What it catches · Before or after potting
SPI: Paste print, before reflow · Before — in line
AOI: Placement and visible fillet · Before — in line
X-ray: Hidden joints under packages · Before — in line or sampled
Electrical test: Continuity, shorts, values · Must be before
Functional test: The board responds to a simulated sensor · Must be before
Dielectric or insulation check: Isolation, if the design has a barrier · Must be before
Visual after potting: Voids, incomplete fill, contamination · After — and it is a cosmetic check only

Read that table as a deadline. Everything above the potting line has to be settled before the compound goes in, because after it you are not inspecting a board, you are inspecting a surface.

### Where the small board creates the test problem

The physical difficulty on this family is access. A board small enough to be heavily panelised has little room for test points, and if the design put the test pads under where the housing sits, they may be unreachable once assembled.

Two practical consequences:

- Test points are a DFM item, not a test item. If they are not on the Gerber in accessible locations, the fixture discussion is over before it starts. Raise it with the layout, not with the assembler after the first batch.
- Panellisation decides whether test is cheap or expensive. Testing in panel form is generally faster; testing after depanelisation means handling a small board with a connector on it. Ask which one the fixture assumes.

### Coating and potting are not the same decision

Buyers often use the two words interchangeably, and they should not.

Method: Protects against · Cost · Reversible · Where it fits
Conformal coating: Humidity, condensation, some contamination · Lower; a mask drawing and a spray or dip step · With effort · Boards that may need rework, larger boards
Full potting: Immersion, vibration, thermal cycling, mechanical shock · Higher; compound, mould or housing, cure time · No · Small boards in harsh locations — this family

On a bumper-mounted board the case for potting is strong. The cost is that you have moved the entire quality burden earlier in the process, and you cannot inspect your way out of it afterwards.

### What to agree before the first batch

- The exact point of no return, written into the process: which tests run before encapsulation, and what the pass criteria are.
- Who owns scrap after potting. A board that fails electrical test before potting is a board. A potted unit that fails at the brand's end-of-line is a disagreement. Agree the attribution before it happens.
- Fill depth and voiding acceptance. "Potted" is not a specification. Fill depth, allowed void size and the visual criteria should be on the drawing.
- Coating mask zones, if coating is used instead — which connectors, which pads, which test points stay clear.
- Whether the compound is chosen for thermal conductivity or cost, because on a sealed board that choice is a thermal decision.

### Where this floor's limits show

Small, heavily panelised boards are ordinary work here, and coating and potting both run in-house. What is not in-house is in-circuit and functional test — the fixture is product-specific and belongs with whoever owns the design. So the sequence question has a specific answer on this family: the electrical and functional proof needs to happen at your end or at a fixture you control, and it needs to happen before the board is encapsulated.

That is not a gap in the assembly. It is the natural consequence of a board that is cheap to build and expensive to scrap.

The parking sensor and headlight driver page (/applications/parking-sensor.html) states the coating and potting capability and the 500 sets to 5,000 sets band. The LED driver (/applications/led-driver.html) has the same potting-before-test problem with a mains barrier on top, and the dashcam sensor carrier (/applications/dashcam.html) is another small board where a step after assembly decides the product. What AOI and X-ray cannot catch (/insights/what-aoi-xray-cannot-catch.html) is the general version of the coverage question.

Decide the sequence before the compound. Afterwards, it is not a process decision, it is a scrap decision.

On an unchanged revision the standard build here is 3 days from kitted parts, which is the number to plan a reorder against rather than a promise about component lead time.

## What is inside a PCBA price — the five lines, and which ones move with quantity

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/pcba-cost-per-board.html
Published: 2026-11-17
Summary: Bare board, component pass-through, placement points, tooling and testing. Four of the five behave completely differently when you negotiate, which is why a collapsed total cannot be audited.

A PCBA price has five parts: bare-board fabrication, component pass-through, placement points × rate, tooling and NRE, and testing. Only two of the five genuinely scale with quantity, and one of them is not the assembly. That is why a 50-piece run costs more per board than a 5,000-piece run without anyone overcharging you.

### The five lines

#: Line · Driven by · Scales with quantity?
1: Bare-board fabrication · Layer count, material, copper weight, board size, surface finish · Partly — panel utilisation improves, but fab has its own minimums
2: Component pass-through · Your BOM, at distributor prices on the quoting date · Weakly — reel and order-multiple minimums dominate small batches
3: Placement points × rate · Number of placements, fine-pitch content, through-hole content · Yes — rate steps down as batch volume rises
4: Tooling and NRE · Stencil, machine program, fixture, panelisation · No — fixed per job, per revision
5: Testing and QA · Inspection coverage, programming cycles, fixture-based test · Partly — test time per board is roughly constant

A quote that collapses these into one number cannot be audited. You cannot tell whether a difference came from the board, the parts, the placement rate or the setup — and those four have completely different negotiating dynamics.

### Which costs are fixed per job, and why that matters at small volume

Four things are charged once, whatever the batch size:

- Stencil — laser-cut, per revision. Changes when the paste layer changes.
- Machine program and feeder setup — per product, per revision.
- First-article inspection — a real cost in engineering time, not a formality.
- Panelisation and tooling — agreed at DFM, fixed for the revision.

Divide four fixed costs by 50 and each board carries a hundred times the setup of a 5,000-piece run. Divide them by 5,000 and they almost disappear. Nothing about the assembly itself changed.

This is the honest explanation of why small batches cost more per board — and it is also why no repeat NRE on an unchanged Gerber and BOM revision is worth more than a few percent off the unit rate. On a reorder, line 4 goes to zero. On a first order, it does not.

### Where reel minimums break the arithmetic

The most under-estimated line is components. Two mechanisms:

- Reel and order multiples. A part may only be sold in a reel of 3,000. You need 47. You buy 3,000, or you buy the reel minimum the distributor offers. The unused remainder is either stocked for you or lost.
- Line-item minimums per part number. Many distributors price a line, not just a part. A BOM with 180 part numbers has 180 chances to hit a minimum.

Which is why a BOM review matters before the quote, not after: consolidating to approved equivalents, and flagging long-lead or end-of-life parts early, changes the numbers more than negotiating the placement rate usually does.

### What a quote should show to be checkable

Six things. If a quote is missing more than two, treat the total as an estimate rather than a price:

- Bare board broken out with layer count, material and finish
- BOM line by line, with the distributor and the price used on the quoting date
- Placement points counted, not estimated, with fine-pitch and through-hole content shown
- Tooling and NRE as its own line, with what it covers and whether it recurs
- Test scope named — what is inspected, what is electrically tested, and by whom
- Assumptions written down — quantity, revision, lead time basis, what is excluded

The last one is the one buyers skip, and it is the one that causes the argument later. "Lead time three days" means nothing until it says from kitted parts, and separately states the component lead time.

### How we quote, as a worked example of the structure

Every quotation we send is itemised against those five lines, with the BOM showing the distributor and the unit price used on the day of quoting. Parts are bought through franchised channels or factory allocation where the part requires it. Shortage lists go out within one working day, and no substitution happens without written approval.

Reorders with an unchanged Gerber and BOM revision carry no repeat NRE. Lead time is stated as three working days from kitted parts, with component lead time called out separately, because that is usually what sets the real shipping date.

If a part can be bought cheaper on the same terms and date, the quote is reworked before the order is placed. That is a checkable promise: you can compare the BOM line against a distributor price yourself.

This note explains price structure, not price levels — those move with quantity, parts and date, and a number printed here would be wrong by the time you read it. For why the fixed lines hurt most at small volume, see why a fifty-piece run costs what it does (/insights/fifty-piece-run-cost.html). For how to order at that size without paying for avoidable work, see ordering fifty pieces of PCBA (/insights/fifty-piece-pcba-order.html).

## What a PCBA quote should contain — and what a bare number leaves out

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/pcba-quote-what-it-should-contain.html
Published: 2026-11-17
Summary: Two quotes for the same board are rarely the same offer. The difference is in what each one leaves unsaid: test, yield, material ownership, and what happens when a part is short.

A unit price answers one question: what does one board cost. A buyer actually needs four answers — what is included, what is excluded, who carries the risk, and what makes the number move. A quote that gives only the first is not wrong; it is just not comparable to anything else.

### The eleven lines

Ask for these as separate lines, not folded into one number. A supplier who can produce them has quoted the job; one who cannot has given an estimate.

Line: Why it changes the comparison
Quantity and revision: A price without the Gerber and BOM revision it belongs to cannot be re-ordered at the same number
Board specification: Layers, thickness, surface finish, copper weight. A quote that does not state it is quoting a default you have not seen
Component cost and ownership: Turnkey (supplier buys), consigned (you ship in), or mixed. This is the largest single variable and the one most often hidden
Component sourcing basis: Authorised distribution, or broker. Same part number, different traceability and different failure rate
Assembly charge: Placement and soldering, split by side if the board is double-sided
Setup and one-time charges: Stencil, programming, first-article. Whether they recur on a reorder matters more than the amount
Test and inspection: Which of SPI, AOI, X-ray, ICT, FCT are included, and which are extra
Yield and rework policy: Who pays for boards that fail inspection, and at what point a board becomes your loss
Coating, potting, conformal: Masking labour is real labour; the quote should say whether it is in or out
Packaging and documentation: Tray, ESD bag, desiccant, lot labels, first-article report
Validity and lead time: Component prices move; a quote with no validity date is not a commitment

### Where the two numbers usually diverge

Material ownership. A turnkey price and a consigned price can differ by more than the parts, because turnkey carries sourcing risk, inventory and obsolescence. Comparing them without stating which is which is comparing two different products.

Test scope. SPI, AOI and X-ray inspect solder joints. They do not power the board. If one quote includes functional test and another stops at AOI, the cheaper one has not covered the same ground — and the gap is real work, not margin.

Yield. A quote that assumes 100% first-pass yield on a board that will not achieve it is a lower number with a hidden second invoice. Ask what happens to the boards that fail.

Setup recurrence. On a fifty-piece run the setup is a meaningful share of the unit price. Whether it is charged again on the reorder, and under what conditions, decides the cost of the second year rather than the first order.

### What to do with a quote you cannot compare

Send the same file and the same question to every supplier, and ask each one to answer in the same structure. Two effects follow: the numbers become comparable line by line, and the supplier who does not answer the structure tells you something useful before you spend a week on samples.

If a quote arrives as one number, the fastest useful reply is not a request for a discount — it is a request to break it into the lines above. On a real job that reply usually changes the number in both directions.

### What we put in a quote

We quote assembly, setup and inspection as separate lines, state whether the components are ours or yours, name the distributor when the part is critical, and say plainly when a test is not run here. On a family page, the panel headed where we are the wrong shop exists for the same reason: a quote that hides a mismatch costs both sides a month.

## How to audit a PCBA supplier in China without visiting the factory

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/pcba-supplier-audit-checklist.html
Published: 2026-11-17
Summary: If the ISO certificate holder and the bank beneficiary are different companies, you are talking to a trading company. That single mismatch settles more cases than any site visit.

Audit five documents before you audit the building: the business licence, the ISO certificate holder name, the bank beneficiary on the proforma invoice, the facility address and the process limits stated as numbers. If the certificate holder and the bank beneficiary are different companies, you are talking to a trading company — that single mismatch settles more cases than any site visit.

### Check 1 — The licence, then the beneficiary

Two documents, one question: does the company you are paying own the plant you are buying from?

Ask for the business licence (营业执照) and read the 统一社会信用代码 — the unified social credit code — along with the registered name and the registered address. Then look at the beneficiary on the proforma invoice. If the beneficiary is a Hong Kong or offshore entity nobody mentioned, stop before any payment and ask why. Payment to a personal account, to a different Chinese company, or to an offshore entity introduced at the last minute is the most common way buyers lose deposits.

Legitimate structures exist: separate trading arms, HK collection entities, group invoicing. But a legitimate structure is explained before you ask, in writing, with the relationship documented.

### Check 2 — The certificate holder, not the certificate

A framed ISO 9001 on the factory wall proves nothing. Four things make a certificate checkable:

- Who is the holder? Compare with the entity on your invoice.
- What is the scope wording? "Manufacture of printed circuit boards" and "assembly of electronic assemblies" are different scopes.
- Which site does it cover? A group certificate and a plant address are not the same thing.
- Is it current, and who accredited the body? Ask for the PDF; check expiry and the accreditation mark.

A worked example, from our own file. The ISO 9001 certificate 38822Q00487R0S is held by Shenzhen Tengmei Technology Co., Ltd. Our registered name is 深圳腾镁科技有限公司 and our English trading name is Shenzhen Tenmay Technology Co., Ltd. Three spellings, one entity — the certificate name is the pinyin romanisation of the registered Chinese name. The unified social credit code 91440300670000384N is what resolves it, not the spelling. Any auditor who cannot explain a name mismatch should be treated as a finding, not a detail.

### Check 3 — Process limits stated as numbers

A supplier who answers capability questions with adjectives is telling you they have not measured. Ask for the numbers, then check them against your design:

Question: A number, not an adjective
Finest passive you place: 01005 (0.4 × 0.2 mm)
Finest IC pitch: 0.30 mm
Largest board: 800 × 480 mm
Daily placement capacity: 300,000 points per day across 8 lines
Minimum order: 50 pcs, same for all three order models
Standard lead time: 3 working days from kitted parts
Workmanship reference: IPC-A-610, class agreed per order

Then the second half of the audit — the numbers they do not have:

Question: Our answer
In-house in-circuit test: No — fixtures run through a qualified partner
In-house bare-board fabrication: No — boards from partner fabs, inspected on arrival
IATF 16949 / ISO 13485: No
Third-party IPC Class 3: No

A supplier who can answer the second table as precisely as the first is either honest or unusually well prepared. Both are good signs.

### Check 4 — Questions that cannot be pre-prepared

These four have no scripted answer, because the answer depends on your files:

- "Open my Gerber and tell me what will not run on your line." A real process engineer names a specific aperture, clearance or panelisation issue within a day. A salesperson says "no problem".
- "What is the first article process for a board at my pitch, and who signs it off?" Look for a role, a document and a photo, not a promise.
- "Show me the last lot record you shipped." Redacted is fine. Nothing to show is not.
- "What did you turn down last month, and why?" If the answer is "nothing", the supplier is either new or not paying attention.

### Check 5 — The record set you should demand per lot

Four documents. If any is missing, the process did not happen in an auditable sense:

- First-article result, with the fixture or stencil ID and the revision it was built against
- Per-serial or per-lot inspection result — AOI/X-ray images attached, not just pass/fail
- Failure log with disposition of every failed board
- Certificate of conformance, with the quantity, the revision and the shipment date

The full boundary list this plant publishes — the four things we do not hold — is on company.html (/company.html), and the numbers in Check 3 are on capabilities.html (/capabilities.html). If you want the same checks done by camera instead of on paper, the companion note is a remote factory audit that proves something (/insights/virtual-factory-audit.html).

## Should one assembler build all three portable power station boards?

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/power-station-three-board-supplier.html
Published: 2026-11-17
Summary: The inverter is the board that decides the product. Keeping it with the BMS removes an arbitration argument; splitting the display costs almost nothing.

A portable power station is three boards: the battery management board, the inverter board that produces the AC output, and the display board that reports state of charge. They share one battery, one enclosure and one certification file. That shared context is what makes the sourcing decision different from the e-bike controller and display, where the two boards answer to different masters.

### The inverter is the board that decides the product

Everything a buyer notices about a power station comes from the inverter. Whether a resistive load starts, whether a motor load trips, whether the output is a clean sine or a modified square, whether the unit hums under a light load — all of it is the inverter control board.

That makes the inverter the board where a build defect is diagnosed as a design problem. A cold joint on a switching device, a bus capacitor fitted with the wrong lead length, a gate resistor that drifted — each one presents to the end user as a product that is not very good, not as a board that was assembled badly. If you split the inverter away from the rest, understand that you have also split the diagnosis.

### What the three boards need from an assembler

Board: What actually decides its build · Cost of splitting it
BMS: Cell sense channels, balancing resistors, protection thresholds; high layer count and fine pitch · Low — a self-contained board with a clear specification
Inverter: Bus capacitance, heavy copper, thermal vias, and the timing of the pure-sine control stage · High — every field complaint about output quality lands here
Display: Low density, a segment or dot-matrix driver, one harness connector · Low — cosmetic, versioned independently

The BMS and the display are both reasonable to source elsewhere. The inverter is the one worth keeping where the rest of the power path is, because the questions you will ask about it are system questions.

### The battery is the reason to couple the first two

The BMS and the inverter meet at one place: the DC bus. Protection thresholds on the BMS decide when the inverter stops being fed; the inverter's inrush decides whether the BMS sees a fault or a load. Tuning that pair is a conversation between two boards.

When both boards come from one assembler, that conversation happens inside one supplier and the buyer receives a tested set. When they do not, the buyer arbitrates, and the arbitration usually consists of forwarding emails between two suppliers who each have a correct explanation.

### What the certification file changes

There is a second coupling that has nothing to do with function: the product certificate. The certificate is issued to the brand owner for the finished unit, and the evidence behind it is generated at build. Which means the record set — reflow profiles, lot traceability, coating records, serial-to-lot mapping — matters here in a way it does not for a simple accessory.

If the boards come from three shops, you need three record sets that agree with each other and a way to tie them to one serial number. That is doable, and some brands do it deliberately. It is simply one more thing the buyer owns, and it should be a decision rather than an accident.

### When one assembler is the better answer

- The batch is small. At 100 sets to 500 sets, three separate setups with three separate first-article approvals is a large share of the total. One set of files, one changeover, one approval is materially cheaper.
- You are still tuning the product. A first or second revision moves between BMS limits and inverter behaviour. One supplier shortens that loop.
- Nobody on your side owns the DC-bus interface. If the interface document only exists in two suppliers' heads, you are one resignation away from losing it.

Split when the display is the only thing changing, when your volumes have outgrown one shop's capacity, or when you have an engineering team that already maintains the interface documentation.

### What to put in the enquiry

- Gerber, BOM and centroid for all three boards, as three sets.
- The output specification: continuous and peak rating, and whether the output must be pure sine. The control stage is not the same board for both.
- Battery chemistry and configuration, because cell count sets the BMS sense channel count and the connector.
- Whether the set is potted or conformally coated, and which connectors stay clear.
- Whether the three boards are one purchase order. A supplier who knows they ship as a set will test them as a set; one quoting three independent lines will not.

The portable power station page (/applications/power-station.html) carries this floor's batch band and the three-board split. The EVSE control board (/applications/evse.html) is the other family on this site where the certification record, not the unit price, is the deciding factor, and the servo drive (/applications/servo.html) shares the same heavy-copper-beside-fine-pitch problem as the inverter. If you are comparing quotes that differ mainly on setup charges, why a fifty-piece run costs more per board (/insights/fifty-piece-run-cost.html) separates the fixed side from the variable side.

On an unchanged revision the standard build here is 3 days from kitted parts, which is the number to plan a reorder against rather than a promise about component lead time.

Last reviewed: 2026-11-17 · Send a board stack for review: WhatsApp (https://wa.me/8617361058693)

## Do you actually need in-circuit test on a robot vacuum mainboard?

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/robot-vacuum-ict-decision.html
Published: 2026-11-17
Summary: Specify ICT and most high-mix floors are out. That is a legitimate choice — but know what you are buying, because ICT proves connectivity, not that the robot works.

Robot vacuum is the densest family on this site: 01005 passives, 0.3 mm IC pitch, double-sided assembly, three to four boards per unit. It is also the family where buyers most often arrive with a test requirement already written into their specification — in-circuit test, on every board. That single line decides which assemblers can quote at all.

### What ICT actually measures

An in-circuit test fixture lands probes on every net through a bed-of-nails interface. It measures connectivity, component presence, component value within tolerance, and orientation for polarised parts. It catches an open joint, a missing part, a wrong value, a reversed diode.

What ICT does not do is prove the product works. It cannot see a firmware fault, a marginal sensor alignment, a motor driver that only fails under load, or a thermal problem. Those belong to functional test, which is a different fixture and a different specification.

So the question is not "do we need ICT". It is "which of these failure modes is our real risk, and which test finds it".

### Where a high-mix floor fits, and where it does not

Test type: What it proves · Where the fixture belongs
SPI: Paste print before reflow · At the assembler — in line
AOI: Placement and visible fillet after reflow · At the assembler — in line
X-ray: Hidden joints: SoC, BGA, thermal pads · At the assembler — in line or sampled
ICT: Net connectivity and component values · Product-specific fixture; not universal to an assembly house
FCT: The board behaves as intended · Product-specific fixture and firmware

The first three are process controls and belong to whoever runs the line. The last two are product-specific: a fixture has to be designed, built and maintained for one design, and it stops being useful when the design changes. That is why many assembly houses — this one included — run SPI, AOI and X-ray in line and quote ICT and FCT per project rather than claiming them as standard.

If your specification says ICT on every board, it is not a criticism of the assembler who declines. It is a statement that the fixture belongs in the build. Say so early and the right suppliers will answer.

### The density problem is separate from the test problem

It is worth keeping these two apart, because buyers often conflate them. A board can be at the limit of what the placement floor handles and still be perfectly testable, and a board can be easy to place and impossible to test without a fixture.

On this family the density is real: 01005 passives and 0.3 mm pitch on both sides means the paste print and the reflow profile carry the yield, and hand rework on a 01005 is usually a scrap decision rather than a repair. That is a process argument for using an assembler who does fine pitch routinely, not an argument about test.

The test argument is different. On a dense double-sided board, the risk you cannot see is under the packages: the SoC, the memory, the thermal pads on the driver side. X-ray covers those. Everything above the board is covered by AOI. What remains uncovered is the electrical behaviour of the assembled unit, and no amount of AOI substitutes for a powered test.

### How to decide, in practice

Ask these four questions in this order:

- What are the field failures we have actually seen? If they are connector and mechanical, ICT will not help. If they are missing or wrong components on a dense board, it will.
- Does the design have test points, and are they accessible on both sides? ICT on a double-sided 01005 board needs probe access designed in, not added later.
- Who owns the fixture? If the assembler owns it, the fixture leaves when you leave. If you own it, you can move the build.
- What is the sample plan? Full ICT on every board and ICT on a first-article plus sample basis are different costs and different assurances. Most buyers who say "ICT on everything" have not priced the fixture maintenance.

A useful middle path on this family: X-ray on every SoC and memory joint, AOI on both sides, and a functional test at the brand's own end-of-line where the firmware already lives. That covers the joints optically and electrically where the pass criteria actually exist.

### What to put in the enquiry

- Gerber, BOM and centroid, plus the layer stack, because double-sided 01005 with a dense SoC is a different profile from a single-sided board.
- Your test specification, verbatim. Not "standard testing" — the actual list. A supplier who receives it can tell you what they run and what they do not, which is the answer you need.
- Annual volume and batch band. This family is normally built in 500 sets to 5,000 sets; below that, fixture cost per board dominates.
- Which board in the stack carries the SoC, because that is where the X-ray and the ICT both concentrate.

The robot vacuum mainboard page (/applications/robot-vacuum.html) states plainly that in-circuit test is not run in-house, which makes it the honest test of whether this floor fits your requirement. The dashcam board (/applications/dashcam.html) carries the same density and the same SoC-under-package risk. What AOI and X-ray cannot catch (/insights/what-aoi-xray-cannot-catch.html) goes through the inspection gap in more detail, and 01005 placement limits (/insights/01005-placement-what-limits-yield.html) covers the yield side.

Ask for the test matrix in writing before the quote. A supplier who answers it precisely has told you where your risk is; one who says "we test everything" has told you nothing.

Last reviewed: 2026-11-17 · Send a test specification for review: WhatsApp (https://wa.me/8617361058693)

## Sharing a build stack between servo drives and VFDs

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/servo-drive-shared-stack-with-vfd.html
Published: 2026-11-17
Summary: One stack, two products, smaller batches. The saving is real; the risk is that a design nobody else can build becomes a supplier with pricing power.

A servo drive and a variable frequency drive are not the same product sold twice. A VFD holds a motor at a speed; a servo holds a motor at a position, and does it thousands of times a second. What they share is a power stage, a gate drive, an isolation barrier and a set of through-hole terminals carrying real current. In sourcing terms, they share a build stack.

### What is genuinely shared

Element: VFD · Servo · Shared?
Power stage: IGBT bridge, DC bus, electrolytics · Often IGBT or MOSFET bridge, DC bus · Yes — same solder and thermal problem
Gate drive: Isolated, one per phase · Isolated, faster switching · Yes in structure, not in tuning
Encoder interface: Usually none, or a simple pulse input · Differential pairs, high-rate, noise-critical · No — servo only
Control: Speed loop · Position and velocity loop · Same silicon, different firmware
Terminals: Mains, motor, braking · Mains, motor, encoder, STO · Yes, and both are through-hole

Two of the four boards in a typical servo — the power board and the control board with the encoder front end — land in the same process window as a VFD. That is why the families are usually built by the same kind of shop: heavy copper, thermal mass, through-hole terminals, conformal coating, batches measured in tens to hundreds of sets rather than thousands.

### The saving from one stack

Consolidating at one assembler buys three concrete things:

- One reflow profile development. A power board with a thick copper pour and a row of electrolytics heats unevenly; the profile is developed per board, not inherited. If the servo power board is a variant of the VFD power board, part of that work carries over.
- One coating specification and one mask drawing. Both families are usually conformally coated. One supplier, one coating material, one set of keep-clear zones.
- One conformance conversation. If both product lines sit under the same quality system and the same documentation, an audit covers both.

At 50 sets to 500 sets per build, those three items are not a rounding error. They are frequently the difference between a quote that works and one that does not.

### Where the consolidation turns against you

The risk is not commercial, it is structural. If one assembler holds the stencil, the programme, the profile, the coating mask and the first-article history for both product lines, then moving the build means re-creating all of it somewhere else. That is a real barrier, and a supplier who understands it may price accordingly.

Three symptoms worth watching for:

- The quote stops moving. When a re-quote on a mature design comes back flat for two years while material moves, the setup has probably become rent.
- The second source cannot be qualified in time. Qualify a second assembler on the simpler of the two boards while volumes are low. It is much easier than doing it during a capacity crisis.
- Documentation lives only at the supplier. The stencil files, the profile and the mask drawing are your product's manufacturing definition. Ask for copies at every revision.

### The encoder front end is the servo-specific decision

Everything else in a servo drive is a VFD problem with tighter timing. The encoder interface is not. Differential pairs at high rate, a shield that has to be terminated at one end and not the other, and a connector that must survive a cable being pulled — that is a four-layer fine-pitch board with a specific routing requirement, and it is where a servo build fails first.

Practical consequences for the enquiry: ask for the encoder board's differential pair routing rules and the stack-up, not just the Gerber. If an assembler treats it as a digital board and routes it like one, the drive will run and then lose position under noise. That failure appears in the field, not on the bench, and it is expensive to attribute.

### When to split

- Different batch bands. If the servo runs at tens of sets and the VFD at hundreds, the changeover economics diverge and the split becomes natural.
- Different customer segments with different audit needs. A machine-tool buyer and a pump buyer do not ask for the same records.
- You need a second source for supply security, and it will only take one of the two products.

### What to put in the enquiry

- Gerber, BOM, centroid and the stack-up for each board.
- Whether the servo power board is a variant of an existing design — if it is, say what changed, because the profile development may be partially reusable.
- Coating type and keep-clear zones, and whether the encoder connector is coated.
- The differential pair specification for the encoder interface.
- Both batch bands, stated separately. This family normally runs 50 to 500 sets; a quote that assumes 500 will look wrong at 50.

The servo drive page (/applications/servo.html) states the shared stack with the VFD family and the 50 to 500 set band. The VFD page (/applications/vfd.html) covers the three-board set and the through-hole work, and the HMI and PLC I/O family (/applications/hmi.html) has the same isolation-discipline problem in a colder thermal environment. For the commercial side of small batches, why a fifty-piece run costs more per board (/insights/fifty-piece-run-cost.html) is the arithmetic.

Two products on one stack is a good position. The mistake is discovering, three years in, that it is a good position for one party only.

On an unchanged revision the standard build here is 3 days from kitted parts, which is the number to plan a reorder against rather than a promise about component lead time.

Last reviewed: 2026-11-17 · Review a drive board stack: WhatsApp (https://wa.me/8617361058693)

## Finding a real PCBA factory in Shenzhen, when half of them are trading offices

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/shenzhen-pcba-factory-guide.html
Published: 2026-11-17
Summary: A trading company is not automatically a problem. Quoting as a factory when you are not one is. Three checks separate the two, and none of them needs a flight.

Shenzhen assembles a large share of the world's electronics, and a meaningful share of the companies presenting themselves as factories are trading offices with a shop floor they visit. Three checks settle it in under an hour: does the ISO certificate name match the company you are paying, can they state a process limit as a number, and will they show you the line on a live call without a day's notice.

### Why the trading company exists at all

It is worth saying first: a trading company is not automatically a problem. A good one consolidates suppliers, handles documentation and saves you a factory relationship you do not have the volume for. Plenty of buyers are better served by one.

The problem is not knowing which one you are talking to, because the two carry different risks:

: Real factory · Trading office
Process changes: Decided on their floor; you can see the limit · Negotiated with a third party you never meet
Quality escapes: Traceable to a lot record they own · Traceable to a supplier who may deny it
Price movement: Component and rate mechanics visible · Margin absorbs the movement, opacity increases
Capacity claim: "8 lines, of which 2 are free next week" · "We have partner factories"

Neither column is dishonest by itself. The failure mode is a trading office quoting as a factory: you buy on the assumption of control that does not exist.

### Check 1 — Certificate name vs company you pay

This is the fastest test and the one most often skipped.

Take the ISO certificate and the proforma invoice, and read the holder name and the beneficiary name side by side. Same name, same entity — good. Different names, ask why in writing, before payment.

Legitimate reasons exist: a Hong Kong collection entity, a group structure, a name romanised differently on the certificate. We are an example of the last one: our certificate is issued to Shenzhen Tengmei Technology Co., Ltd., our registered name is 深圳腾镁科技有限公司, and our English trading name is Shenzhen Tenmay Technology Co., Ltd. The unified social credit code 91440300670000384N is what links all three — and we publish the mapping so nobody has to take it on faith.

The illegitimate version is a beneficiary that appears at the last minute, is offshore, or is a personal account. That is where deposits disappear.

### Check 2 — Can they state a process limit as a number?

Ask three questions and listen for numbers:

- "What is your finest IC pitch?" → 0.30 mm is an answer; "fine pitch capable" is not.
- "What is the largest board you place?" → 800 × 480 mm is an answer.
- "What is your daily placement capacity?" → 300,000 points per day across eight lines is an answer, and it is checkable against the machine count.

A trading office can repeat marketing numbers. What a trading office cannot do is assign the work to a line, a machine and a shift. So follow up: "Which line would this board run on, and what else is booked on it that week?" The answer either refers to their own schedule or it does not.

### Check 3 — The unannounced live call

Not a video they sent you. A call you schedule, where you choose the targets while the camera is walking.

Ask to see:

- The X-ray station, with someone reading an image on screen
- The SPI screen showing the job currently on the line
- The feeder cart for a live job, with a reel barcode visible
- A lot record for the batch on the floor, opened in front of you
- The coating booth, with masking prepared for a real board

None of these can be improvised in five minutes in an office. All of them can be shown in a factory that is actually running.

### What Shenzhen does not give you

Say the limits out loud, because geography is not a capability:

- Certification is not implied by location. Shenzhen has plants at every level, from one manual bench to fully automated. The address tells you nothing about the certificate.
- Not every board should be built here. If your programme needs IATF 16949 inside a vehicle chain, ISO 13485 for a medical device, or in-circuit test under the assembly roof, choose a plant that holds those — including if that plant is not us.
- Cheap quotes at high volume are a different business. Above a few thousand pieces a month, a larger plant's hourly rate usually beats a small-batch specialist. That is arithmetic, not loyalty.

### What we publish, so you can check it against the list above

Check: Our published answer
Legal identity: 深圳腾镁科技有限公司 · USCC 91440300670000384N · trading as TENMAY
Certificate: ISO 9001, 38822Q00487R0S, holder name Shenzhen Tengmei Technology Co., Ltd.
Finest pitch: 0.30 mm · finest passive 01005 (0.4 × 0.2 mm)
Largest board: 800 × 480 mm, double-sided
Capacity: 8 × Yamaha YSM20/YSM10, 300,000 points per day
Minimum order: 50 pcs, same for turnkey, partial turnkey and consigned kit
Lead time: 3 working days from kitted parts
Not held: IATF 16949 · ISO 13485 · third-party IPC Class 3 · in-house ICT/FCT · bare-board fabrication
Live audit: Available on request, unscripted, targets chosen by you

If any line here does not match what you see on a call, treat that as the most important data point in the whole exercise.

The document checks in this note are compressed into a checklist on the supplier audit page (/insights/pcba-supplier-audit-checklist.html); the camera checks are expanded on a remote audit that proves something (/insights/virtual-factory-audit.html). The entity record itself sits on company.html (/company.html).

## The 800 mm board is not the hard part of a treadmill build

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/treadmill-large-board-mechanics.html
Published: 2026-11-17
Summary: Buyers worry about board size and get caught by a console harness and a motor drive in a sealed plastic housing. Here is where to spend the attention instead.

A treadmill is two boards — a motor drive board in the base and a console board on the handlebar — plus a harness that runs the length of the machine through a frame that flexes under a running load. Buyers arriving at this family usually ask about board size first. Size is the easy part.

### What the size limit actually constrains

The motor drive board can run to the largest panel this floor handles, which is a real capability boundary: it decides which line the job can be assigned to and whether it fits at all. That is worth confirming before anything else, because a design that does not fit has no other question.

But once it fits, board size stops being the risk. A large power board is heavy copper and thermal mass; the profile is developed per board rather than inherited, and that is a one-time engineering task with a known cost.

### Where the failures actually are

Failure: Where it starts · Detectable at the assembler?
Console goes dead or flickers: Ribbon harness or connector lift after the handlebar is tightened · Partly — a pull test on the connector, not AOI
Motor drive overheats: Thermal path in a sealed plastic housing; electrolytic life · No — housing-level design, not board
Speed reads wrong under load: Current sense path contamination or a marginal shunt joint · Partly — visible joints yes, drift no
Incline or speed drifts: Connector contact resistance after vibration · No — appears in service
Board works, safety key fails: Key switch is a harness and enclosure item · No — not a board function

The pattern is consistent: the failures that generate service calls are mechanical and thermal, and the ones your inspection can see are the ones that rarely fail. That is worth knowing before you spend the quality budget in the wrong place.

### The connector is the product

On this family a connector that lifts when the console is bolted down reads as an intermittent fault that no AOI will ever find, and it will be attributed to the board. Two process items reduce that:

- A stated insertion and pull requirement on the console connector, checked at first article.
- Strain relief designed in, not added as a note. If the harness hangs off the connector with nothing taking the load, the joint takes it instead.

Most treadmill boards that come back from the field are not badly soldered. They are mechanically over-stressed at one connector, and the solder did what it was told.

### Thermal, inside a closed plastic base

The drive board sits in a base with limited airflow, and the electrolytics on it have a life that is a function of temperature. The board's contribution is thermal vias and copper area under the switching devices; the housing's contribution is whether the heat has anywhere to go.

This is a DFM conversation, not an assembly fix. If the design was thermally signed off on a bench in free air, the first summer is the real test. Worth raising at DFM: what the maximum expected ambient in the base is, and whether the capacitor choice assumed it.

### The two boards are built in different worlds

The motor drive is a power board: heavy copper, through-hole terminals, thermal vias, conformal coating because the base sees sweat and dust. The console is a light board with a display, buttons and a long harness, versioned for cosmetics.

They also move at different speeds, like the e-bike pair: the console changes when the brand wants a new look, the drive changes when the motor or the deck does. Quoting them on separate lines is what keeps a console restyle from reopening the drive approval — and at 200 sets to 2,000 sets, sharing one setup across both is worth asking about if they ship together anyway.

### What to put in the enquiry

- Gerber, BOM and centroid for both boards, plus board dimensions stated explicitly so the panel fit can be confirmed.
- The maximum board dimension if the drive board is near the size limit — this decides line assignment.
- Coating requirement and keep-clear zones, including the terminal blocks.
- The console connector specification: part number, insertion force, and how it is strain-relieved.
- Expected ambient in the base, so the thermal question gets answered at DFM.
- Whether both boards ship on one purchase order, since that changes setup allocation.

The treadmill and fitness control board page (/applications/treadmill.html) states the two-board split, the largest panel size carried and the batch band. The VFD family (/applications/vfd.html) is the closest process relative — heavy copper beside a fine-pitch control board — and the e-bike controller (/applications/ebike.html) repeats the pattern of a power board and a cosmetic board on one shipment. Why a fifty-piece run costs more per board (/insights/fifty-piece-run-cost.html) explains the setup arithmetic that decides whether sharing one setup is worth it.

Confirm the board fits, then spend the rest of the attention on the harness and the heat. Those are what come back.

Last reviewed: 2026-11-17 · Send a board pair for review: WhatsApp (https://wa.me/8617361058693)

## Quoting a VFD as three boards or as one set

Source: https://tenmaypcba.com/insights/vfd-three-boards-one-quote.html
Published: 2026-11-17
Summary: Line-by-line tells you where the money is; set pricing tells you what a drive actually costs to build. Ask for both, then decide which number you are managing.

A variable frequency drive is three boards with three different process profiles: a control board with isolated gate drive, an IGBT power board carrying the DC bus and current sensors, and a keypad board. A drive missing one board is not shippable. That single fact drives the whole quoting decision.

### Two ways to price the same build

Approach: What it answers · Where it misleads
Three separate lines: Where the cost sits: which board carries the through-hole work, which carries the coating, which is trivial · You cannot tell what a shippable drive costs
One set price: What a drive costs to build and ship · It hides an expensive board inside a blended number
Both, with the set as the commercial unit: Everything above · Nothing much — it just takes more paper

Buyers usually ask for one or the other. The useful enquiry asks for both, because they support different decisions: the line breakdown is what you need to redesign cost out, and the set price is what you need to plan a purchase order.

### Why the set is the real unit

The keypad board is small and cheap until it is not. Membrane tails, a segment or dot-matrix driver and one harness connector: low value, high nuisance. A wrong footprint there turns into a hand-reworked batch and the drive still cannot ship.

Compare that with the power board, which may run up to the largest panel this floor handles and carries the IGBT stage, the DC-bus electrolytics and the current sensors. It is heavy copper, large thermal mass, through-hole terminals and bus bars that must be soldered without cooking the devices beside them.

Three boards, three very different cost drivers, one shipment. If a supplier quotes you a keypad price and a power board price but cannot state a set price, they have not priced the thing you are buying.

### The reorder question is where set pricing pays

On drives, the demand shape is not consumer growth. It is spare-board and maintenance orders arriving in tens and hundreds rather than thousands, and a build measured in days rather than weeks. The buyer's real question is "how fast can I restock a drive", not "what is the cheapest board".

Which is why the first-order quote and the reorder quote should be separated in the paperwork. The band here is 50 sets to 500 sets. The first order pays for stencil, programme, profile development and first-article approval. The reorder, on an unchanged revision, does not. A supplier who keeps the programme and the approval on file can quote a reorder against that same revision, and the number drops for a reason that is visible rather than negotiated.

### What the through-hole content does to the price

Drives carry terminal blocks, relays and bus connections that have to be hand or selectively soldered. A pure placement house subcontracts exactly this step, which is why drives are a comfortable fit for a floor that runs it in-house and a poor fit for one that does not.

Two questions expose this quickly:

- Is the through-hole work done in-house, or subcontracted? If subcontracted, the schedule has a second party in it.
- Is conformal coating done in-house? Drives usually specify it; masking connectors and test points by hand is real labour, not a rounding error.

### What inspection proves here, and what it does not

SPI runs before reflow on the fine-pitch side, AOI after reflow, and X-ray on the IGBT and thermal-pad joints where voiding under a power device is invisible from the surface and presents later as a hot drive.

What none of it proves is that the drive works. In-circuit and functional test with a load bank are not assembly operations — the pass criteria belong to the firmware and the motor. If your process requires full functional test at the assembler, that is a different supplier category, and saying so early saves both sides a month.

### What to put in the enquiry

- Gerber, BOM and centroid for all three boards, plus the stack-up for the power board.
- Which board runs to the largest panel size, so the line assignment can be confirmed against the size limit.
- The coating requirement and which connectors and test points must stay clear.
- First-order and reorder quantities separately, since they are priced differently and honestly so.
- Whether a set price is available, in addition to the three lines.
- Whether functional test is expected at the assembler. Ask it explicitly; do not let it be discovered at handover.

The VFD and inverter page (/applications/vfd.html) states the three-board split, the batch band and the standard build time from kitted parts. The servo drive family (/applications/servo.html) shares the power stage and adds an encoder front end, and the treadmill control board (/applications/treadmill.html) is the other family where the largest board size is the deciding capability. Why a fifty-piece run costs more per board (/insights/fifty-piece-run-cost.html) is the arithmetic behind the first-order versus reorder gap.

Ask for the set price. Then ask what the second order costs. The two numbers together tell you more about a supplier than either one alone.

On an unchanged revision the standard build here is 3 days from kitted parts, which is the number to plan a reorder against rather than a promise about component lead time.
